#4867. The 6 Best Pillows of 2026, Tested by Editors

The $190 Purple Harmony Pillow might be divisive, but it earned our best overall badge.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

As someone with frequent neck pain, I would give up my cozy sheets, white noise machine, and sunrise alarm clock if it meant I wouldn’t wake up with a stiff neck. (And that’s coming from someone who invests a lot in their sleep.)

"I think that a pillow can make a big difference in people that have a history of neck issues," says Leia Rispoli, MD, an interventional pain management specialist and physiatrist at DISC Sport & Spine Center. This is the very reason why I tend to lug my favorite pillow around on weekend trips.

There isn’t one pillow that works for everyone. Your best option depends on your sleep position, preferred firmness, body type, and whether you tend to overheat at night. To find the best pillows, our editors and testers slept on popular models from Purple, Casper, Coop, Saatva, and other leading sleep brands. We evaluated each one for comfort, support, temperature regulation, adjustability, ease of care, and value.

I love the Purple Harmony Pillow so much that I try to convert nearly everyone who mentions sleep within earshot of me. I even pack it for overnight trips. But it does feel unusual at first. Inside, a springy, ventilated latex core is wrapped in Purple’s GelFlex Grid, a flexible, honeycomb-shaped layer that bends under the weight of your head and springs back when you move. Together, these materials make the pillow feel buoyant rather than sink-in like memory foam.

I tested the medium, 6.5-inch loft, meaning the pillow’s height before it is compressed. It provided enough height to support my head and neck while I slept on my side without feeling rigid. The materials give slightly beneath heavier areas, which helped reduce uncomfortable pressure around my head and neck. As someone who frequently experiences neck and back pain, I consistently felt comfortable and supported while sleeping on it.

Purple recommends the low, 5.5-inch version for most stomach and back sleepers. The medium and tall versions are generally better suited to side and combination sleepers, who often need more height to fill the space between the head and mattress. Body size and personal preference will also affect which height feels most comfortable.

The Harmony was also one of the coolest pillows I tested. Air circulates through the ventilated latex and open honeycomb layer instead of becoming trapped inside a solid block of foam. Its stretchy outer cover is also designed to draw sweat away from the skin so it can evaporate. Even on warmer nights, I rarely felt the need to flip the pillow over in search of a cooler surface.

After nearly three years of regular use, my pillow has not developed noticeable lumps or gone flat. Its durable build helps justify the high price, but there are compromises. The pillow is unusually heavy, and some sleepers may notice the grid’s texture through the cover. Purple’s 30-night trial is also shorter than the trial periods offered by many competing brands.

Still, no other pillow I tested delivered the same combination of responsive support, cooling, and long-term shape retention. I would purchase it again without hesitation.

Women’s Health art director Christine Giordano typically sleeps with two or three pillows, but the Casper Original gave her enough support to use fewer. “This pillow gave me the support I needed while still feeling light and airy,” she says. “It was breathable and didn’t clump, keeping me cool and comfortable at night.”

The Casper uses a pillow-within-a-pillow design: A firmer inner cushion provides structure, while a softer outer layer adds cushioning. Both layers are filled with polyester microfiber, a synthetic material made to feel light and fluffy like down. The construction prevented Giordano’s head from sinking too deeply while still giving the pillow a plush feel.

Giordano tries to sleep on her back but usually shifts onto her left side during the night. The pillow remained comfortable and supportive in both positions, making it a strong choice for combination sleepers who alternate between their backs and sides. However, stomach sleepers or people who prefer a flatter pillow may find its approximately nine-inch uncompressed height too lofty.

The breathable cotton cover and airy synthetic fill also prevented the pillow from feeling stuffy during testing. It’s not as breathable as a dedicated cooling pillow, but Giordano did not notice heat buildup or need to flip it over for a cooler surface.

The entire pillow is machine-washable, which makes it easier to clean than models with foam or latex cores. Its soft filling may need occasional fluffing to maintain its shape, but Giordano did not notice clumping during testing.

At under $100, it is one of the more affordable pillows we tested. Giordano liked it enough that she replaced some of the other pillows in her home and purchased additional Casper ones for her family.

Women’s Health executive health and fitness director Jacqueline Andriakos, CPT, calls the Coop Original Adjustable the most comfortable pillow she has tried. “I’ve never been a pillow snob or had major issues with basic pillows from Amazon, but I noticed that this was far more comfortable than other, cheaper pillows I’ve used,” she says.

The pillow is filled with a blend of shredded memory foam and microfiber. Memory foam molds around the head and neck, while the soft synthetic fibers keep the pillow from feeling like a dense, solid block of foam. Unlike a pillow with a fixed height, the Coop can be unzipped so you can remove filling for a flatter feel or add more for extra support. The process can get messy, but that adjustability makes it easier to tailor the pillow to your body and sleep position.

Coop offers the pillow in classic, crescent, and cut-out shapes. Andriakos tested the classic and cut-out versions while switching between side and stomach sleeping. She preferred the cut-out, which has a curved indentation that creates room for the shoulder and allows the pillow to sit closer to the neck.

“I liked that it could wrap around my neck and shoulders, and I could almost cuddle it like a body pillow with an arm threaded underneath,” she says. Although the shape can look slightly awkward inside a standard pillowcase, it was super comfortable when she slept on her side.

The pillow felt plush, but Andriakos’ head did not sink so deeply that her neck felt unsupported. She also found the outer cover breathable, although sleepers who regularly overheat may prefer a pillow specifically designed for cooling.

Because its height can be adjusted, the Coop can work for side, back, stomach, and combination sleepers. Side sleepers will generally need more filling to keep the head level with the spine, while stomach sleepers may prefer to remove enough filling to create a flatter surface. Finding the right amount may require a few nights of experimentation, but Coop’s 100-night trial gives you time to make those adjustments.

It would take an exceptional pillow for me to consider replacing my Purple Harmony, but the Saatva Latex Pillow gave it serious competition. Although both pillows contain latex, they feel noticeably different. Purple uses one solid, springy latex core, while Saatva uses shredded pieces of latex surrounded by a soft layer of fine synthetic fibers. This gives the Saatva a plusher, more traditional feel, but it has enough structure to support the head and neck.

The pillow feels dense when you first pick it up, but my head settled gently into the soft outer layer without sinking too deeply. The shredded latex inside quickly returned to its original shape when I moved, so the pillow stayed supportive as I shifted positions. As a side sleeper who frequently experiences neck pain, I did not wake up with additional stiffness.

Saatva offers two heights. The standard version measures approximately four to five inches and is designed for back and stomach sleepers who generally need a lower pillow. The high-loft version measures approximately six to seven inches and is better suited to side and combination sleepers who need more height between their heads and mattresses.

I also appreciated that the pillow remained breathable throughout the night. The small spaces between the pieces of shredded latex allow air to circulate, while the cotton cover feels cool. It does not create the immediately cold sensation of a cooling pillow, but I did not notice uncomfortable heat buildup.

The outer layer is filled with microdenier fibers, which are very fine synthetic strands designed to imitate the light, fluffy feel of down. You can machine-wash this outer layer and its cotton cover, but the inner latex core must be removed and kept out of the washing machine.

At $165 for a standard/queen size, this is one of the more expensive pillows we tested. Saatva also provides only 45 days for returns, which is shorter than the trial periods offered by several competitors. Still, its combination of plush cushioning, responsive support, and breathable materials makes it an excellent choice for sleepers who want a luxury-hotel feel that’s still supportive.

For hot sleepers, a breathable pillow can be the difference between a good night’s sleep and a night spent tossing and turning. The Slumber Cloud UltraCool stood out because its cooling effect was immediately noticeable during testing.

Women’s Health managing editor Laura McLaughlin described the sensation as “a little sci-fi” because the surface felt immediately cool when she rested her head on it. The cover contains Outlast, a material designed to absorb excess body heat when you become warm and release it as your skin cools. This helps prevent heat from collecting around your head and face, although the effect may be less noticeable beneath a thick pillowcase.

McLaughlin also found the pillow easy to combine with others. “It’s great for layering with other pillows to get just the right height,” she says. “It’s neither too dense nor too high to use in combination with others already in place.” That makes it especially useful for sleepers who want additional height without placing a rigid pillow beneath their heads.

The interior is filled with polyester down alternative, a synthetic material designed to imitate the airy feel of down. It is available in soft/medium and medium/firm versions, allowing sleepers to choose how plush or structured they want the pillow to feel. The softer option will generally suit stomach sleepers or anyone who prefers more sink while the firmer version may provide better support for back and side sleepers.

The entire pillow can be machine-washed, a convenient advantage over pillows with foam or latex cores. However, synthetic filling can begin to clump after repeated use and washing, so it may require regular fluffing to redistribute the material.

Although the UltraCool does not provide the customized support of an adjustable pillow, it delivered the most noticeable cooling sensation of any model we tested.

The Brooklinen Down Alternative Pillow is built for sleepers who want the fluffy feel of down without actual feathers. It’s filled with recycled poly microgel, a cluster of fine synthetic fibers that creates a light cushioning similar to down.

Unlike many pillows that come in only one firmness, this one is available in soft, medium, and firm versions. Brooklinen recommends the soft pillow for stomach sleepers who generally need less height beneath the head; the medium for back sleepers; and the firm for side sleepers who typically need more support to fill the space between the head and mattress.

Its cotton sateen shell feels smooth and has a subtle sheen. The pillow is also certified by OEKO-TEX Standard 100, which means its materials have been tested for a list of regulated substances. That certification does not evaluate the pillow’s comfort, durability, or environmental impact.

Brooklinen allows most products to be returned within 365 days, although it deducts a $9.95 return fee from the refund. That’s one of the most generous return windows we’ve seen.

The pillow can be machine-washed in cold water and tumble-dried on low with wool dryer balls until completely dry. As with most pillows filled with loose synthetic fibers, it may require regular fluffing to redistribute the fill and preserve its shape.

A pillow’s height, or loft, should keep your head and neck aligned with your spine. Side sleepers generally need a taller pillow, back sleepers a medium-height pillow, and stomach sleepers a low pillow. Your mattress matters, too: The more deeply your shoulders sink into it, the less pillow height you may need. Most of the pillows we tested fell in the five- to nine-inch range, offering different levels of support depending on their material and sleeping position.

Side sleepers often benefit from a medium-firm or firm pillow that maintains its height. Back sleepers generally need medium support while stomach sleepers may prefer something softer that compresses easily. Because firmness labels vary by brand, consider the pillow’s material and height as well.

“There isn't one brand that's the magical brand for everyone,” says Rispoli. Look for a pillow that supports your head without tilting your neck sharply upward or downward. Adjustable pillows can help you fine-tune the height. Consult a health care professional if your pain is persistent, severe, or accompanied by numbness or weakness.

Memory foam molds around the head but may retain heat. Latex feels springy, breathable, and durable. Down is soft and airy but may lack structure while synthetic down alternative is usually easier to wash but may flatten over time. Hybrid pillows combine materials to balance cushioning and support.

Look for ventilated latex, shredded filling, or another construction that allows air to circulate. Some covers also absorb excess body heat or feel cool, although a thick pillowcase may reduce the effect. People who sleep cold may prefer denser foam or plush down filling that holds slightly more warmth.

As a sleep writer, I’ve tested all kinds of sleep accessories, from mattresses to eye masks, but pillows are probably my most-tested product category. (Unfortunately, I once tested so many pillows at the same time that I injured my neck, but I’ve learned my lesson.) To find the best pillows available online, I selected popular picks from leading sleep brands, like Purple, Casper, Saatva, Pluto, and more, for testing. Some helpful testers and I have slept on these pillows for dozens of nights to determine whether they’re worth the money, and our top pick has been my favorite pillow to sleep on for nearly three years. From flat pillow lovers to hot sleepers, our diverse crew of sleepers tried out eight pillows of various styles, materials, and price points.

#4866. 6 Best Bamboo Sheets That Mirror Silk, Tested by AD (2026)

If you love the slight sheen and smooth feel of silk bedding like me, my guess is that bamboo sheets are probably up your alley too. The natural material can make your bedroom look elevated, and you won’t actually have to pay for pure silk or satin.

What makes bamboo sheets so popular is that they’re also just as good for hot sleepers: They have moisture-wicking properties, are hypoallergenic by nature, and feel cool to the touch (no disrespect to linen lovers). The lightweight weave also has a lovely drape to it. For a dramatic look, especially in a dark and moody color palette like this Upper East Side family home, these sumptuous sheets can’t be beat.

I’ve put on Sleep Week for the last couple of years, where AD editors share the essentials for styling a bedroom. Needless to say, I’ve tried a lot of sheets from our roster of beloved bedding brands to match my ever-changing space. I arguably have too many sets to count, some new and some old, to give my space personality—and my colleagues can say the same. After all this research, I can confidently share this concise list of our all-time favorites in the bamboo category.

For consistency, all of the prices reflect queen sizes. However, many brands reach up to a king size.

Cozy Earth is a personal favorite of mine for bamboo sheets—the brand’s bread and butter. They’re so breathable—even when I layer with a thick down comforter on top and throw blanket at the foot of the bed when it’s cold outside or when my AC is blasting—and have deep pockets to fit my notoriously tall mattress and topper combo. My taste just so happens to overlap with Oprah’s, if you’ve peeked at her Favorite Things list recently, which feels like a good omen, too.

I’m not the only fan, this set has earned the top overall pick in this story because pretty much every Shop AD writer, editor, and contributor who’s tried the Cozy Earth bamboo sheet set stands behind it for a few reasons: It is temperature-regulating, long-lasting (even after several cycles in the washing machine), and some of the softest bedding out there. Contributor Yelena Moroz Alpert calls her relationship to Cozy Earth a “borderline obsession” because of the natural fibers and neutral colorways that give the bedding an “earthy sophistication.” Shopping editor Audrey Lee calls the sheets “super light and airy, so it’s mostly a summer staple.”

Contributor Megan Wahn adds that the set is a favorite of hers because it feels much more expensive than it actually is: “I honestly thought these sheets were silk when I first slept on them, that’s how smooth and buttery soft they feel.” I love the walnut shade since my bedroom leans more moody, but if you’re into a clean, neutral shade like 2026’s color of the year, Cloud Dancer, I recommend the white or gray color for a calm, minimal bedroom. Their shore set is another style for anyone who likes a more coastal look. But Alpert says it best: “Not sure how Cozy Earth does it but the sheets feel like velvet without being heavy.”

Quince is the luxury-on-a-budget brand I’ve become pretty familiar with over the last two years of trying their duvets, sheet sets, and even their bath towels—and the bamboo sheets don’t fall short. Breathable bedding is a must for my sleep setup, and I’ve been a little surprised by how well I sleep through the night with this set. It feels smooth and cool to the touch, but still cozy enough to bundle up with during the winter months. One of my best friends is a hot sleeper, so whenever he visits, I use these (and the matching bamboo duvet cover) to make his bed. He says these truly keep him at a comfortable temperature throughout the night, so he’s never throwing the covers off mid-REM sleep.

This is the brand I’d recommend if you want to style your bed to a tee. I have the bamboo sheets in a warm terracotta hue to give my bedroom a serene, almost desert Airbnb-like aesthetic in the summertime. There are almost a dozen neutral and vibrant earth tones to match your bedroom’s design, though. These points, on top of the sub-$150 price tag, earned them a top spot in this list. However, if you’re like me and wear oily sheet masks and use thick body butters at night, you might notice some light staining on the sheets.

Because of their glossy sheen, these Luxome sheets probably look the closest to silk out of all of the picks in this list. I have the bedding in a truffle color, but what makes this option so unique are the jewel tones available, like sapphire, that are hard to find with other brands. The generous size of these sheets (they have a 17-inch pocket depth) gives them an even more elegant drape for a glam bedroom.

The neutral tones are compelling, too. For Sleep Week this March, the Shop AD team and I explored how to design a bedroom with a narrative, so we designed rooms inspired by classic novels. One of those storybook sanctuaries took inspiration from Dune, and I think Luxome’s sheets (which happen to have the same name) have a cool, chrome-like finish for fans of futuristic Sci-Fi novels like this one. All in all, these are also soft and breathable, a welcome relief for me when I’m combating hot NYC days.

Yes, we like heritage brands that have been acclaimed for ages at AD, but we’re always on the hunt for new and budget-friendly brands that are worthwhile, too. Sijo launched an Amazon-exclusive line a few years ago that offers a luxe feel and sustainable material sourcing at a lower price point. This basic Doz by Sijo set of bamboo sheets is another staple for my sleep setup. My skin has gotten pretty sensitive over time, and I love how soothed I feel when I sink into these sheets. They have a little more of a polished texture than other picks in this list, so I glide into bed. It’s hard to tell the difference between these and other high-end picks on the market by virtue of their material; it feels like a softer, less slippery satin. The pockets aren’t as deep as Cozy Earth’s, and the colors aren’t as striking as Quince’s burgundy and terracotta options, but for the price, I say it’s still a nice and simple set to shop.

Even though contributor Blake Bakkila prefers more textured bedding like linen, she says Cariloha’s “Aloha” bedding has been a saving grace to keep her cool. “These were the perfect sheets to layer on our bed during a heat wave that rocked Southern California, and they only got softer with each wash,” she shares. After Bakkila and her husband adjusted to the supple texture, she says the “temperature-regulating bamboo” sheets have been a great choice to keep in rotation since they’re “exceptionally smooth and lightweight” with a “cooling effect.” Keep in mind that these are truly thin sheets and almost have a transparent appearance. So if you’re looking for bedding that’s a bit weightier, the Quince or Cozy Earth in this list might be a better way to go.

These sheets are made of 100% bamboo infused with what Bearaby calls “smart botanicals,” including extracts like peppermint and marine proteins. They don’t feel sticky like some silky sheets can when it’s hot outside—they’re airy and refreshing to sleep on and the minty essence only enhances the feeling of freshness. These botanicals do more than smell good—they eliminate up to 99.9% of bacteria directly within the fabric. As your heat rises, the botanicals activate to cool you while keeping the material clean. And—to answer the million-dollar question—the sheets do live up to their “second skin” name—the fabric is so soft and fluid, it feels like it's melting on my body.

Here at Shop AD, we don’t test sheets in a lab—we test them in our very own homes. Why? Because that’s where you’ll be using them too. Each of the sets in our Best Of roundups has been washed, dried, and slept on for countless nights by one of our editors to ensure that they’ve put them through the ringer. The sets are selected to reflect a variety of price points, materials, and styles, and we pride ourselves in giving each set firsthand, real-world use.

Whether you’re a bamboo bedding faithful or it’s your first time exploring the category, there are a few factors I recommend keeping in mind below.

When it comes to the world of linens, bamboo fibers are made from the bamboo plant, which requires far less water than cotton and regrows quickly, so bamboo sheets are often considered one of the more eco-friendly options available. There are few popular bamboo materials: bamboo viscose, rayon, and lyocell. All are antimicrobial, soft to the touch, and absorbent. Depending on if and what they are blended with, they can take on more linen- or cotton-like properties. Here’s a breakdown of each:

The fabric’s weave will change the texture, softness, and general propensity for wrinkling. Below, here are more details on the two most popular weaves: twill, sateen, and percale.

To keep laundry day simple, the bedding in our list simply requires a machine wash and tumble dry. We generally recommend washing on cold and drying on low, as these gentler settings can help preserve the bedding’s quality. However, be sure to check the labels on the sheets for any specific care instructions.

While all bamboo sheets do a superb job of temperature regulating, your best bet (for overall comfort plus silkiness!) is to find a 100% bamboo viscose or lyocell set—like the Cozy Earth pick—with a thread count between 250 and 350, made with a sateen or percale weave. This typically indicates a durable weave that won’t wear easily over time.

As enthusiasts for all things interiors, we recommend looking for bamboo sheet sets that come in colors, prints, and patterns that can match your bedroom’s design. So, if you lean more minimalist, try neutrals like ivory. If you love maximalist style, go big with bold designs and hues—from embroidered details to splashy colors like terracotta or butter yellow.

You can usually find a set of this bedding type between the $50 to $400 range. To get the most out of your purchase, we recommend looking for eco-friendly certifications to help make sure your sheet set has the best quality. For example, the Oeko-Tex Standard 100 applies to bedding that is free of harmful chemicals.

In essence, yes—but how much so really depends on the quality of your set. Bamboo bedding is known for being cool to the touch overall, but the weave itself will ultimately determine the breathability of the sheets. Keep an eye out for bamboo sheets with a 300 thread count weave or above, as our editors mention that these typically have the most airflow for a good night’s rest.

Is Bamboo Viscose Better Than Egyptian Cotton?

Bamboo sheets, because of the strength of their fibers, actually have better longevity than cotton sheets, and offer superior moisture-wicking and temperature regulation to cotton sheets. Bamboo, especially bamboo viscose, also brags a smoother, more soothing feel against the skin compared to cotton, which can require more washes to get the the super soft or silky feel you desire.

Yes! The nature of bamboo is hypoallergenic, making bamboo bed sheets perfect for those with sensitive skin, eczema, or anyone prone to allergies. Bamboo’s super-fine fibers inherently resist things like dust mites, mold, and mildew. Even at the molecular level, it’s a moisture-wicking material, helping you stay sweat-free while also creating an environment inhospitable for dust mites (that need moisture). The fibers are naturally smooth, too, making for a soft sleeping experience.

How Do Bamboo Sheets Compare to Linen in Terms of Softness and Durability?

In our experience, both materials are durable when the sheets are made of 100% natural fibers instead of blends, but bamboo sheets are much softer. Unless it’s stonewashed, linen is usually known to feel a bit scratchy at first and then soften with wear and care. Bamboo sheets are softer down to their microscopic makeup, as their very fibers are smoother than linen.

Shop favorites from Brooks, New Balance, Dr. Scholl’s, and more.

The New Balance 608 V5 Trainer has over 38,000 Amazon reviews, and for good reason. The brand integrated its signature ABZORB midsole, designed to reduce joint impact during walking through its cushioning and compression resistance. Plus, they come in narrow, standard, and wide sizing.

Lined with mesh for ultra-breathable comfort, the Pegasus is a winner thanks to its slim, low heel that helps maintain a smooth walking cadence. We love that the 42 is lighter than the previous model and has a curvier toe box that gives more toe spring, a smoother ride, and a roomier fit.

#4864. 7 Best Moroccan Rugs, Vetted by AD Editors (2026)

The Moroccan rug is one of the easiest ways to add texture and intrigue to any room. Originally made to protect floors against the harsh cold of the Atlas Mountains, we see these lush, woolly carpets as a staple in the modern design world because of the range of color and style options available. The rug type has become synonymous with traditional undyed cream colors, vibrant jewel tones, and geometric patterns. It’s no wonder they pop up across tons of our home tours—like this artful Brooklyn studio and floral Victorian house—and have become a favorite among artists like Claudio Bravo and celebs like Patrick Dempsey.

Boucherouite, the hand-weaving technique employed to make these rugs, was created by semi-nomadic Amazigh tribes, and the style can be found in abundance in the busy souks of Marrakech. Now, with many direct-to-consumer and vintage Beni Ourain-inspired styles on the market, the perfect Moroccan rug is just one click away. With all the options at your disposal, it may be intimidating to know where to start. Fear not, we’ve rounded up a few top picks below along with advice on how we’d style them.

Give your guests the coziest welcome with this Azilal rug from Revival Rugs. Its long, narrow design makes it ideal for tight entryways. And while the oblong diamond pattern speaks to geometric patterns you’ll see across traditional Moroccan rugs, the pink tassel is a niche, colorful detail that won’t overpower surrounding decor. This is an authentic hand-knotted Moroccan rug, with wool locally sourced from the Atlas Mountains. Because of its small size, you may also consider hanging it up to add a textural element to your wall decor.

Break up the monotony of home office decor by placing an eclectic rug under your desk setup. While the soft grey and subtle design still create a distraction-free workspace, the cheeky oxblood hues add a touch of personality to make you smile between emails and Zoom meetings.

You don’t have to get a custom carpet straight from Marrakesh to have a high-end rug. The Saira rug from Quince is a handwoven option at an affordable price. The geometric motif is heavily inspired by Moroccan design and the medium-pile, hand-spun wool is designed to feel plush under your feet.

Calling all maximalists and color drenchers. #4863. Could Your GLP-1s Make You Blind? Here’s What to Make of the FDA’s Latest Notice.

For years, there have been rumblings and even research about a rare but serious condition that’s been linked to taking a GLP-1 medication. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is doing something about it.

The FDA just released a drug safety communication to warn patients and healthcare providers about the potential increased risk of developing non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) when you take a GLP-1 medication. NAION is a rare condition that can lead to vision loss in one eye, and it can be permanent.

Again, this isn't the first time concerns have been raised about the risk of NAION. But it is the first time the FDA has issued a warning about it.

Given that up to 11 percent of Americans currently take a GLP-1 for weight loss, this news stands to impact a lot of people. How concerned should you be if you're one of them? Eye experts and a doctor who prescribes GLP-1s break it down.

Meet the experts: Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system; Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute; and Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

The FDA's notice is designed to flag the potential risk of NAION to people who use GLP-1s. The FDA also notes that the agency will require all manufacturers of GLP-1 medications to add information about the risk of NAION to the Warnings and Precautions section of their labels.

"Patients and caregivers should be aware of a potential increased risk of NAION, a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss, with GLP-1 RA use," the notice reads.

The agency cited a 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology as well as its own meta-analyses and retrospective cohort study in the notice. They also noted that “NAION cases have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1 RA products.”

However, the complication remains rare: incidents from the FDA’s meta-analysis were just 6.4 events per 100,000 per year for patients using the medications.

The warning is just that—a warning to patients and physicians that this could happen, explains Joseph Rizzo, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear, a member of the Mass General Brigham healthcare system. "Most outcome-related issues in medicine should be thought of as being probabilistic—there is a certain chance that events can occur," he says. "This warning indicates that the FDA has reason to believe, at least at this time, that the probability of NAION occurring is higher in patients who take GLP-1 RA drugs."

But Dr. Rizzo stresses that there's no evidence that these drugs cause NAION—just that there's a link.

So…why issue a warning if it's not proven that GLP-1s cause NAION and it's so rare? "The severity of a complication matters alongside its frequency," says Bavand Youssefzadeh, DO, an ophthalmologist with Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles and a cofounder of the Global LASIK and Cataract Institute. "Even a rare risk deserves attention when it can permanently affect vision." The warning is likely designed to give healthcare providers a heads-up that it could be NAION if a patient has symptoms, he explains.

"It's their duty to report any adverse effects, just so people are aware of them," says Mir Ali, MD, the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California.

While NAION is scary, doctors say it's important to put the data in perspective. "It's extremely rare, but it can happen," Dr. Ali says. Given how much GLP-1s can help with blood sugar management, weight loss, and downstream health effects, Dr. Ali says that the risk of NAION is "not a reason not to seek these medications."

Dr. Rizzo agrees. "I essentially never discourage the general use of GLP-1 RA drugs," he says. "Ultimately, the risk-to-benefit assessment must be decided by the patient, but physicians should provide sufficient information to the patients to better inform their decisions."

People should stay aware of the risk without panicking, Dr. Youssefzadeh says. "It's also worth remembering that the people most likely to be prescribed these drugs—people with diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnea—already carry a higher baseline risk for NAION, so the risk isn't starting from zero," he adds.

#4861. The Surprising Staying Power of Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy

A24’s Club Kid makes the case for the comedy’s unlikely legacy—and social relevance—in 2026.

EARLY ON IN Jordan Firstman’s dramedy Club Kid, druggie-with-a-heart-of-gold Peter has to shepherd his surprise 10-year-old son through an apartment party. Despite knowing each other for just a few hours, the club promoter and his child hold hands as he guides the way through the bacchanal. It’s a metaphor—what isn’t these days?—and it’s also kind of a recreation of a key sequence in Adam Sandler’s Big Daddy.

In that movie, 5-year-old Julian “Frankenstein” McGrath (played by young Dylan and Cole Sprouse) holds his hand aloft before he steps off the sidewalk, looking for help from his newfound father.

Replace McDonald’s breakfasts with coke and ketamine (plus a Charlie Kirk reference), and A24’s Club Kid is the clear heir apparent to the 1999 Sandler comedy. I’m far from the first person to make the connection. IndieWire’s David Ehrlich’s first-impression response was to ask: “What if A24 made a gay Big Daddy?”

It may seem like an odd movie for a brand like A24 to mirror. However, Big Daddy is somehow the film from the peak Sandler run that has had the longest shelf life. In fact, it may be the late ’90s–early 2000s comedy with the best depiction of the 2026 way of life. For better—or for worse.

Despite the fact that it was a hit at the box office, Big Daddy was reviled at the time of its release, even winning Sandler a Razzie Award for Worst Actor.

And, sure, it’s not the most elegant film—with its near-incessant Hooters jabs and Rob Schneider’s catastrophic accent—but still, it’s managed to stick around in the public consciousness for nearly 30 years. And it’s not just Ehrlich and I who think so.

“I particularly loved Big Daddy. That was my number one,” Paul Thomas Anderson said on an episode of The Bill Simmons Podcast in 2017 when asked about casting Sandler in his film Punch-Drunk Love. “It was a little bit more polished; it was able to be sincere and [mix in] the crazy fucking dirty shit that Sandler likes to do and got the mix really right.”

In Club Kid, promoter Peter (Firstman, who wrote, directed, and stars) somehow ends up in charge of a precocious kid while flailing in both romance and his career. Peter, like Sonny, has to instantly shift his lifestyle, one that only functions when you have little to care for, including yourself. Both protagonists need an act of God to abandon their early-30s doldrums.

And honestly, it’s a sentiment that a lot of people my age (including myself) can relate to.

At the tail end of October, The New York Times published a story (which, thankfully, my parents haven’t sent to me yet) titled “Can’t Afford a Home. Can’t Afford a Baby. Can’t Afford Life. This Is 30.” The gist is that millennials feel burned out now that they know they’re unlikely to achieve the luxuries earlier generations enjoyed.

“In the past, the idea was that you would check all these boxes by 30, give or take. But the more I think about it, so much of that is incredibly out of reach,” says one source in the article. Even decades ago, Sonny Koufax would have probably agreed with the article, before ripping out part of the newspaper to clean up some spilled milk next to his third bowl of cereal of the day. Both films find the hearts at the center of their respective protagonists’ messy, work-in-progress stories. Is there anything more 2026 than that?

When you watch Big Daddy in 2026, you almost forget how much of a schmuck—but vulnerable too—Sandler allowed Sonny to be. I was pleasantly surprised that Sandler ultimately loses his chance at raising Julian by himself. It’s a small, complicated victory for a movie that uses a schlocky, heartfelt monologue about fathers to reach a contrived moral coda, but we’ll take our wins where we can get them.

#4860. A Brooklyn Townhouse Celebrates a Forgotten Design Pioneer

In the early 1920s, the Pittsburgh-based manufacturer Armstrong Cork Company (now Armstrong World Industries) made the prescient move of tapping a young arts educator named Hazel Dell Brown to act as its in-house decorator. Hers would be an under-recognized yet wildly influential career. Over the course of more than three decades, she designed countless rooms for advertisements, booklets, catalogs, and more that showcased the brand’s products, chief among them linoleum flooring. With their bold colors, fearless mix of patterns, and daring pastiche, her interiors shaped an entire generation of homes in the Rust Belt and beyond.

For two contemporary artists setting out to renovate a Brooklyn town house for their young family, Brown’s little-known work recently served not only as inspiration but also as a litmus test. When interviewing architects to take on the project, the couple first presented examples of vintage Armstrong schemes. “A lot of people would take one look and then show me something different,” reflects the wife, who learned about Brown while working on a project in Pittsburgh. Not so in the case of Tal Schori and Rustam Mehta of GRT Architects. The AD100 duo instantly responded to Brown’s surface-heavy approach and inward-facing embrace of small spaces, or as Schori puts it, “rooms within rooms.” As for their interior designer, Penelope August, a friend of the wife’s since preschool—she implicitly passed with flying colors.

A circa 1980 Gio Ponti chandelier crowns the living room, which is furnished with a vintage Vladimir Kagan sectional sofa and a Jens Risom chair upholstered in a custom fabric based on a Macgregor Harp painting; artwork by Rose Marcus and wallpaper by Antoinette Poisson.

The kitchen features art-glass cabinet fronts by Paul Wissmach Glass Company and a custom terrazzo floor inspired by ancient roman mosaics of unswept debris.

Hembus wallpaper in a custom blue distinguishes the primary bedroom; painting (above bed) by Michael Wang.

The project evolved into a dynamic collaboration as the couple and their team gutted the town house, set in Carroll Gardens and previously renovated in the 1990s. Together they took care to preserve historic details like the original doors and staircase, with its original mahogany newel posts and handrails. Wherever appropriate, they embraced imperfections, filling in the gaps between old floorboards with contrasting tinted epoxy and leaving levels ever so askew. “This house shows signs of age and that’s not a bad thing,” says Schori. Adds Mehta, “As artists, they understood what is and isn’t precious so that the home does not feel overly restored.”

The backyard was updated by Brook Landscape, with a shed and swing set by GRT Architects.

In the son’s room, shaker-style cabinetry reveals a reading nook.

A refurbished tub from The Demolition Depot anchors the primary bath, which is lined in tiles by Balineum (on walls) and Artistic Tile (on floor).

Brown was nothing if not a gleeful problem solver, presenting flexible solutions to the needs of everyday life, often through inventive secondary spaces. (“Your rumpus room can be anything you like” proclaimed one Armstong campaign.) True to that strategy, GRT devised a floor plan full of versatile surprises. Adjoining the dining room is a cave-like lounge for watching television or just relaxing, with a pass-through to the kitchen for the easy arrival of snacks. Opposite the cookspace—more on that showstopper later—is a cozy breakfast area, with a load-bearing skylight that offers glimpses of the roof terrace (and sometimes curious children) above. And on the second level, a secret passage leads from the primary suite into the library, one column of shelving concealing a door. “All these appendages to the main spaces allow multiple things to happen at once,” says Schori.

In the daughter’s room, Shaker-style trim is painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Ground.

The kids’ bath mixes terrazzo walls with custom floor tiles by Haand.

Oak millwork incorporates vintage Piero Fornasetti panels in the dining room, where Guillerme et Chambron chairs surround an antique farm table; painting by Jo Nigoghossian, and custom fireplace fabricated by Daniel Armitano.

Surfaces and furnishings tend toward the eclectic and one-of-a-kind, with a mix of wallpapers and fabrics, some deadstock, setting the stage for vintage treasures. In the living room, a Vladimir Kagan sectional sofa found at auction doubles as a jungle gym of sorts. The primary bath is anchored by a salvaged earthenware tub, since glazed a light blue to complement the retro checkerboard tiles and scalloped vanity. And the dining room’s custom millwork incorporates a series of midcentury Fornasetti panels. Doorknobs, lighting, motifs, art by their circle of creative friends—it’s all a mishmash. “We liked things independently of how they worked together,” says the wife. Adds August: “It was so fun to stitch all these elements into an old house—I love a space where you come upon something unexpected.”

A detail of the kitchen’s terrazzo floor shows stone and metal shapes (some abstract, some legible) inspired by detritus.

A custom sofa frames the lounge off the dining room, which has a pass-through to the kitchen; carpet by Stark.

In the living room, a Gretta Johnson painting hangs above the fireplace, which is flanked by artworks by Cletus Johnson (left) and Ted Mineo (near right) and Miles Huston (Far right).

The husband’s office/music room is cocooned in cork; painting (at left, bottom) by MacGregor Harp.

The stairwell’s painted checkerboard floor hints at classic Americana.

Floor to floor, the mood shifts. The son’s and daughter’s rooms each riff on classic Shaker woodwork, with rails and built-in cabinetry that respond to the exposed ceiling joists. Enlivened by a splatter-painted floor and celestial configuration of ceiling lights, the plywood-lined attic operates as a kids’ club, craft room, and family theater in one. (How’s that for a rumpus room, Hazel?) Thanks to some clever excavation and engineering on the part of GRT, the combined garden level and cellar is now a double-height studio for the wife, complete with a gantry crane for hoisting heavy sculptures. Outside, meanwhile, Brook Landscape transformed the backyard into a romantic swath of greenery.

Vintage globe lights from a one-time optometry office add a surreal touch to the powder room.

Loose arrangements of greenery frame the steps to the backyard.

GRT Architects combined the garden level and cellar into a double-height art studio with a register of exposed brick.

A vintage Vilhelm Lauritzen ceiling light punctuates the primary bedroom; painting by Margaux Ogden.

As for that kitchen, here the team took inspiration not only from Brown but from two additional touchstones. Cabinet fronts nod to art glass at the Upper East Side’s late great Glaser’s Bake Shop, the salvaged interiors of which August and the wife chanced upon at The Demolition Depot. The floor, meanwhile, riffs on ancient Roman mosaics of unswept detritus, an example of which can be found at the Vatican Museums. “We wanted a kitchen that wouldn’t look bad if it got messy,” says the wife. Working closely with GRT and August, she and her husband evolved that historic precedent into a contemporary series of shapes, some abstract and some legible (a knife, a carrot, a wine glass). Rendered in scraps of stone or metal, their forms now appear to float in poured terrazzo.

“The way artists think about objects and architecture is as a constant work in progress,” says Mehta. “These are visual people with an incredible mental library of references.” Would Brown approve? Without a doubt. As the designer once wrote: “Whatever you do, use your own ideas. Don’t be afraid of them.”

But, especially as a style writer, half the fun of the holidays is having a good excuse to put together a good outfit.

My family’s Thanksgiving gatherings tend to be pretty casual, so I’m not one to show up in anything overly dressy or uncomfortable. I’m usually somewhere in the middle, opting for an outfit that looks like I made an effort but still lets me enjoy a second helping of stuffing without worrying about a too-tight waistband. Think a great sweater with loose-fitting jeans, a knit dress with boots, or even a smartly-styled leggings outfit. Because as much as I love dressing up for the holidays, I also want to enjoy post-dinner card games or sit comfortably on the couch afterward.

If you’re approaching Thanksgiving dressing the same way, I’ve rounded up six outfit ideas to help get you inspired. I’ve included a few options perfect for a Christmas card photoshoot, along with more laid-back looks that are just as fitting for a casual family gathering. No matter what your holiday plans look like, these outfits strike that happy medium between looking good and feeling comfortable. Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have some mac and cheese to make.

In my opinion, there’s no outfit more perfect for the holidays than a sweater dress and boots. It’s cute enough for family photos but loose and soft enough to keep you comfy all day (especially if you kick the boots off at the door). Grab a long-sleeve knit dress that hits somewhere between mid-thigh and the knee and pair it with some fleece-lined tights and your fave knee-high boot. A midi or maxi dress with an ankle bootie works too.

Start by pulling out a denim jacket and denim skirt. From there, add a plain white T-shirt. I love brown for the fall, so I wore my version of this outfit with brown boots and a matching brown belt and bag. I love this combo because it looks super stylish, but I don’t feel overdressed or uncomfortable when I wear it. Don’t have a denim skirt or jacket? No problem. You can recreate this look with a leather jacket, jeans, or any neutral mini skirt.

Start with a pair of satin or silk pants and pair them with a sweater and ballet flats in the same shade. This outfit has been one of my go-tos lately because it’s so comfortable, but the monochrome palette and shiny finish of the pants make it look like I tried way harder than I actually did. You can even make it feel a little dressier by swapping the flats for a pair of pointed-toe ankle boots.

It doesn’t get comfier than leggings and slippers. For ultra-casual gatherings when you just want to focus on family and food without looking frumpy, just style yours a little smarter. Go for a pair of leggings with minimal seaming (especially a pair without a front seam), which makes them look sleeker. Then grab a dressy-looking oversized sweater—something with a boxy cut, a turtleneck, or a nice knit. I find that my tweed stitch J. Crew Rollneck Sweater is perfect for this look. Finish it off with a neutral slipper and a pair of scrunchy socks.

#4858. What “Food Is Medicine” Actually Means, According to a Cardiologist

Plus, Chef Marcus Samuelsson shares easy ways to sneak more plant-based foods into your diet.

Despite what fitfluencers and gym bros might have you believe, eating healthy is about a lot more than counting macros and calories. Every day, scientists are learning more about how our eating habits can influence health beyond just our weight, including blood pressure, cholesterol, blood sugar, and risk of developing heart disease.

That's part of the idea behind a buzzy approach to health care known as “food is medicine,” which contends that what we put on our plates can be a meaningful part of preventing and managing disease.

The challenge is understanding what actually helps and turning that knowledge into meals we want to keep eating. To unpack this, Future You host and editorial director of Men’s and Women’s Health Rich Dorment sits down with Marcus Samuelsson, the acclaimed restaurateur and author of the new cookbook, Back to Green, and Louai Razzouk, MD, a cardiologist at NYU Langone Health.

Here’s a look at some of the themes covered in the episode:

Samuelsson says that beso is an Ethiopian drink that combines roasted barley with water or milk of your choice. “You just shake it and this is the best protein shake you can have,” he says. You can find the more specific recipe in Back to Green.

He grew up eating foods like beso as well as shiro, a stew made from chickpea flour, and other Ethiopian “superfoods” that he incorporates into his dishes today.

Dr. Razzouk says it doesn't mean that you can treat a disease with food alone. “It does mean that you may be able to prevent it by having a healthier and more balanced diet, and possibly minimize how many medications you need to be on,” he says.

Dr. Razzouk says that while you may still need to be on medication, food can make a “huge” impact when it comes to managing conditions like diabetes or high cholesterol. “Food impacts our level of inflammation, our insulin sensitivity, our weight,” and our blood pressure, he says.

The first warning sign that a patient’s diet may be less than ideal is if they get most of their food from Uber Eats or another delivery service. “Most of the stuff that we order in, especially living in New York City, contains a lot of saturated fats, a lot of added salt, and a lot of processed food,” he says. He discusses a couple more red flags in the episode, including meal timing.

In his early 20s, traveling in Southeast Asia and Singapore opened his eyes to a new way of eating—and the idea that there’s great food to be found all over the world.

A plant-forward diet doesn't have to exclude animal protein, he says, pointing to the Mediterranean and DASH diets as examples of eating plans that incorporate some meat. “What I tell patients is that typically if you have a choice between getting a source of protein from an animal source versus from plants, then I would try to get it from plants,” he says.

“What I tell patients is that I want you to enjoy your life,” Dr. Razzouk says, adding that fad diets typically don’t work. “What we would like you to do is find a balance,” he says, eating in a way that's enjoyable and that benefits your health.

It's a lentil salad with a coconut turmeric vinaigrette—and Samuelsson breaks down why the flavors work so well together, plus ingredients you may have in the fridge or pantry that can level it up even further.

He’ll often bring home new ingredients (e.g. spirulina) and encourage his son to look up the health benefits before they cook with it together.

Dr. Razzouk says diets high in fiber not only may lower your risk of colon cancer, but they also may lower your level of LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, which impact your risk of cardiovascular disease. It also helps keep you full.

Cooking together can be an enjoyable family activity, Samuelsson says. “When I cook waffles and pancakes with my kids, we have fun,” he says. “The kitchen is a mess, but iPads are down, we're spending time together.”

Samuelsson suggests chickpeas, sea moss, and the fruit soursop. Dr. Razzouk suggests nuts (walnuts in particular) and extra-virgin olive oil.

#4856. This Is Still the Best Water Bottle I've Ever Used

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

YOUR WATER BOTTLE is an expression of yourself. Sure, you're buying the thing for its functionality and design, but you’re also buying into what the water bottle represents. Whether you’re in need of an all-metal wide mouth for outdoor trekking, an insulated squeeze bottle for home gym power hours, or a smart water bottle that can track your daily intake, we've got the best water bottle to fit your hydration needs below.

Most importantly, you're buying a water bottle to nourish your body and give it the liquid it requires. Now, precise water intake depends on the person and how active they are. We do know that it's not always easy to throw back the H2O, but the benefits are many and there are easy tricks to drinking more water, which will only benefit the body. Having a high-functioning, reusable water bottle you enjoy using will keep you high-functioning as well.

As a study last year found, most adults are not getting enough in terms of daily water intake. That may seem trivial, and perhaps even equate to fewer trips to the bathroom, but there are real health concerns there. Proper hydration can reduce the risk of disease and injury, aid with recovery, and much more. So, let us embrace making it as easy as possible to get the right amount of water we all need.

The Yeti Yonder water bottle has been a go-to for several of our editors for a few years now. The chug spout and cap design is perfect for everyday use, not too narrow or wide. The BPA-free plastic construction is so tough that it's been through drops onto concrete from 10 feet high (it accidentally fell off the top of an SUV when one editor was visiting family in Kansas City). Another big reason why we chose a plastic water bottle as our best overall pick is due to weight—the Yonder is much lighter than its metal counterparts. Unless you're doing some serious hiking or camping, the Yonder will essentially serve multiple uses without any questioning of keeping liquid cold or durability.

The Yonder hardly ever leaks either, no matter which cap you choose. We personally like the add-on Yonder Tether Cap. It makes the bottle a little more streamlined and takes off even more weight. But, the traditional cap it comes with is solid too and might actually be easier to carry by itself. And we've found the 25 oz size to be the sweet spot.

Last detail to point out is price and number of colors available. Sometimes Yeti gear can get expensive. This is not the case with the Yonder water bottles. Pick and choose from all the new colors the brand releases over time. Build a small collection. Gift a few. This is our favorite water bottle we've used over the years.

This is a more practical version for on-the-go guys who want to see what the Stanley craze is about. The slim design makes it slide into backpacks and gym bags with ease, and its pop-top cap is simple and secure. The cap design actually uses a two-step locking process to help avoid accidentally opening (which is a huge plus for those of us who've used these types of water bottles in the past). But it's not like cracking a safe, as the thing opens with relative ease for that quick pull of water when you need it right away.

The Quick Flip Go's double-wall-insulated design means it can keep cold drinks cold and hot drinks hot. One of our editors has even used it to sip morning coffee from time to time. We imagine it would even keep some white wine chilled in a backyard setting, too.

So why is this water bottle not our top pick? It comes down to weight. The Quick Flip Go is just a tad heavier than the Yeti Yonder. If you can get over the weight detail, though, then this pick is just as valid as a top choice.

Can a water bottle be playful? The radiant color scheme here suggests so. And why not, this is the tool that should accompany you on a lot of joyous outings, from cycling through country roads to hiking in the woods. Choose from a host of three sizes (24 oz is our preferred capacity) and enjoy the FreeSip Spout, which pivots to and from big gulps and sipping from a straw seamlessly.

The carry loop is ergonomic and folds into the bottle and push-button access means no leaks. While relatively slender overall, we found that the bottle had no problem taking on scoops of ice with the lid fully off. And once that ice is in place, you're set for 24 hours of polar temperatures. About the only scenario in which this bottle struggles is for athletes competing in helmet sports, as the broad mouth can't get through a lot of face guards. But you could also just take that helmet off before hydrating.

With so many rave reviews in favor of this bottle, it was a little hard to approach it as a skeptic. But that's what good testers do, and we came in thinking there was no way it could match the hype. Almost immediately in our testing we were proved wrong. This is a contemporary water bottle for the contemporary world and once you have one, you never want to go back to the old way.

Why does it slap? Aesthetic, durability, and a high-functioning nature. The handle is one of the best we've used, the build is sturdy, and the associated app is all kinds of helpful. It self-cleans in a single minute, insulates for a full day, and there's even a hydration tracker to keep you swigging when you should be.

The handle is detachable and the bottle itself filters the contents, making for a clean sip every time. The look is among the best out there and the color options are great too. Complaints? Few and far between, although the drinking sensors can be a little buggy and the nozzle is tricky to clean. But overall, it's a gem.

Basic squeeze water bottles for the gym are okay for use, but if you're looking for a much more enjoyable way to stay hydrated while working out then you'll want to try the Camelbak Podium. This water bottle is under $20 (sometimes even lower depending on the sale) and comes with an insulated design that keeps cold water from covering the outside of it—which means no condensation will be soaking your hands in between sets.

The spout and cap design is another huge sell for why we love the Podium for the gym. The top is designed to keep away dirt for mountain bikers, but when transferred to the gym it means there's no leakage when falling over and no gross gym dust and germs floating where you put your mouth. The spout is also similar to drinking out of a Camelbak backpack, which a few of our editors found novel.

The Podium is a little outside the box for what you'd think of as a gym water bottle, but its insulation and high level of leak-proofing makes it seriously good for all types of active settings. It doesn't hurt that it has a cool design, too.

Familiar, durable, and affordable is what makes Nalgene so good after so many years. The brand offers a ton of fun colors, designs, and patterns, so you have a full array of ways to express yourself. However, we realize the design of your Nalgene might not matter as much if you plan on layering it with all the cool stickers you collect on your travels.

Does it have insulation or specialized cap designs for sipping? No, but that's not the point. Nalgene water bottles are all about keeping things minimalist. Over time, it might start to leak a little bit or get beaten up by the dishwasher. If that happens, find a way to recycle and buy a new one for less than $20. Overall, this is a modern classic of a water bottle that's about as durable as they come. We've even run them over with mountain bikes and small cars and didn't even put a dent in 'em. The simplicity means it's also noticeably easier to clean.

Toughness with a simple design that appeals to the bare-bones hydrators out there. We like to think they’re just old enough now they’ve become somewhat iconic, earning a following for all camps, from classroom commuters to weekend warrior backcountry hikers.

If there was a water bottle we might want to bring to a deserted island, this might be it. That's because it excels in versatility, able to do just about whatever you need it to do. We appreciated the wide mouth, which delivered big swigs after long jogs or paddles on a SUP. There was never any spilling thanks to a leakproof spout and the hinge lock is a nice accent, especially if you're on the active side and like to have your water bottle with you on those adventures.

The extra large clip is nice for outings like hikes and travel and we found the insulation to be pretty good, keeping things chilled for at least 12 hours even in warm conditions. It's easy to clean, whether by hand or in the machine, and it fits in every cup holder we tried, from cars to strollers. If you need an extra nudge of insulation, just pack the thing with ice. We found the bottle to be a bit weaker than others in terms of durability (can dent up if you're hard on the thing) but for the price, it's a nice option indeed.

You really can't go wrong with any Hydro Flask, but this 32-ounce water bottle came to be our favorite from our editors who like to hike and camp, and from those who enjoy a high-capacity water bottle. The wide mouth design at the top makes for fast drinking as well as easy pouring and cleaning. As for the material, you've got insanely durable stainless steel with double wall insulation at your service.

This water bottle fits well in most hiking backpacks and duffel bags, despite its larger size. We liked how secure the cap and handle are too, as it allows for one-handed carry when walking short distances.

You're buying excellence with this water bottle. It's going to stay strong for years, no matter what adventures you throw at it. Outdoorsy types especially should consider this model if they're in need of a water bottle.

We liked the first edition of the Hidrate Spark PRO and the second round only improves on the original. It’s an entire hydration program tied to an ultra contemporary bottle and helpful sibling app. You can customize your intake based on your activities and track your progress right down to the drop.

The bottle itself is sweatproof. We appreciated the fact that it rarely if ever slipped out of our paws, even amid a grueling workout. The double-insulation does its job and the recycled 18/8 stainless steel is a nice touch. Also, the lid performed well, even outdoors, with a protective lid, a large carrying handle, and a chug spout for when you’re really thirsty.

When you get a higher IQ bottle such as this, it can sometimes be a little demanding, Not the case here. The newest option from Hidrate does insist that you stay hydrated, but in subtle fashion, with the occasional glow or beep. It’s much better than a bottle that nudges too hard, causing the user to revolt and ignore the thing.

Smart as this water bottle is, it still requires some babying when it comes to washing. The sensor is especially sensitive and should be cleaned with care. But that’s a small price to pay for a water bottle that essentially serves as your personal hydration coach.

There are a handful of filtered water bottles on the market, but no brand has wowed us more than LifeStraw. For starters, the LifeStraw filter is one of the most trusted designs on the market. According to the brand, the two-stage filtration will eliminate 99.999999% of bacteria (including E. coli and Salmonella), and 99.999% of microplastics, sand, and dirt. LifeStraw then packed its filter inside the stainless steel bottle, which we found to be much more appealing than plastic models where you can see the filter inside.

The cost of the Lifestraw Go here is a little elevated, but you are paying for the special filter. You do need to change the LifeStraw filter inside about every 60 days, so that's an extra cost. The payoff though, from what our editors discovered, is the peace of mind you get filling up your water bottle at a public water fountain or from tap water that comes out of a sink.

Grab this water bottle if you're looking for a filtered option with excellent design. There are times when you can’t fully trust your water source but this vessel affords peace of mind (and no bickering of the gut).

To say these bottles were tested is an understatement. Over the course of several years, various Men's Health editors and I put them to work—like, overtime. We paired them up with the most active members of our team, allowing us to get a clean picture of just how well these bottles perform. Hot weather, cold weather, in the gym, out on the trail, on the saddle of a bike, on plane rides, or just commuting; we brought them everywhere.

Throughout the process, we paid close attention to various attributes. Obviously, we wanted a water bottle that looks good. But more importantly, we wanted a water bottle that made staying hydrated easy, thoughtless, and perhaps even enjoyable. We analyzed design, material, size, and special features. We waded through reputable reviews and talked up insiders in the outdoors recreation and sporting worlds for their takes. And of course, we looked at price.

In the end, the Yeti has won us over on all fronts. Durable, lightweight, packable, and super affordable, it has been a favorite among many testers since it released in 2022. But several others came close, offering different traits like filtration, improved insulation, or more sophisticated lids.

Some people prefer wide-mouth tops on their water bottles for faster drinking, while others prefer a spout design that's much smaller and easier to sip. Really it comes down to preference, but there are spout designs we tested that are more enjoyable to drink from than others. Do keep in mind that lots of companies make tops that are interchangeable in case you want to switch to a different design.

To avoid any contamination of plastics, most water bottles we reviewed came in a metal design. There are some plastic water bottles we tested, however, that were BPA-free and we found to not have any impact on taste. Our top-tested water bottle from Yeti is actually made from BPA-free plastic. Our editors have tested this water bottle for nearly two years and have found no issues with taste or with material breakdown from a dishwasher.

Material also dictates temperature retention, with things like double-insulated stainless steel keeping things nice and chilled for long periods of time. Plastic tends to not insulate quite as well, but can be quite durable (and recycled). Keep this in mind as you weigh how important an ice-cold pull of water is to you.

How much water are you going to need? Capacity is a vital consideration, as you might just be looking for a little hydration while at work (where you can continue to refill when necessary) or be out and about all weekend at the campground, potentially away from a water source. Less volume is just fine for quicker outings or when you want to be streamlined, like on a bike. But you'll be wanting additional capacity for, say, lengthy conferences, road trips, or exhausting workout routines.

There are a few water bottles we selected thanks to special features our editors love. Lifestraw, for example, provides some of the best water filtration you can buy. The fact Lifestraw discreetly hides its filter behind a stainless steel body is a huge reason why we featured it on our list. The same goes for the Camelbak Podium, as its insulated body and cap and spout design make it especially suitable for indoor gym settings.

Yes. A reusable bottle is easier on the planet for that very reason—it's reusable. Single-use plastic is wasteful stuff and, worse, it does not decompose, likely ending up in the ocean and your food supply chain (not to mention turning into microplastic). Going with a bottle like the ones listed here does require some energy and inputs upfront, but because it's your long-term bottle (don't go losing it now), the carbon footprint is less.

You can take it a step further by purchasing a bottle made with responsibly sourced materials, sometimes even made from up-cycled or recycled materials. Look for non-BPA (a bad chemical) options and preferably ones that use very little if no plastic. Glass and stainless steel are generally easier on Mother Earth. And be good to yourself by keeping the thing clean and sterile.

Here's the thing about mold: It likes wet environments. You know, like inside of your water bottle. It's a repulsive thought, but some of that gunk buildup in your vessel might just be mold. Don't fret, you can clean the thing.

Now, it would take a fair amount of mold to sicken the average person but regardless, a clean water bottle is just worth having. Wash your bottle daily, either in the dishwasher if it's permitted or by hand, ideally with hot water and a scrub to get into those nooks and crannies—water bottle brushes are a great tool.

Occasionally, consider a more intense clean. Do to the bottle as you might to your coffee maker, soaking it in a mix of vinegar and water. Even the occasional boiling water soak will help keep the bottle pristine.

#4855. PMOS, Formerly PCOS, May Be Associated with Alzheimer's Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), formerly known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), has been linked to changes in brain function and cognition that may overlap with those seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

However, a review published October 13 in the Journal of the Endocrine Society suggests that metabolic conditions commonly associated with PMOS, rather than PMOS itself, may help explain a potential link to Alzheimer’s disease and dementia risk.

“Researchers are exploring whether some metabolic conditions commonly seen in women with PMOS, such as insulin resistance, obesity, type 2 diabetes, [and] elevated cholesterol, could play a role in dementia, since these are already known risk factors for cognitive decline,” Yesika Garcia, MD, board certified endocrinologist with Medical Offices of Manhattan, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline.

“In other words, any potential connection may be related to these underlying metabolic issues rather than PMOS itself. I think it’s important to clarify that an association does not mean causation,” she added.

The researchers searched PubMed for studies published through 2025 examining brain structure and function, cognitive performance, biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, and dementia risk in people with PMOS.

Because PMOS is a newer term, the researchers searched for studies using both PMOS and PCOS.

The review identified studies suggesting that people with PMOS may experience mild differences in certain cognitive abilities, including:

Some brain imaging studies using MRI and PET scans identified differences in brain structure and function among people with PMOS. Researchers also observed hormonal changes associated with differences in gray matter.

Some studies identified elevated biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease in people with PMOS. These findings appeared to overlap with metabolic changes seen in type 2 diabetes, particularly those associated with obesity and insulin resistance.

The researchers also found that neurological differences were less pronounced when people with PMOS were compared with metabolically healthy control groups, suggesting that associated metabolic conditions may play an important role in these findings.

Overall, the review suggests that metabolic conditions associated with PMOS may contribute to changes in brain health, although more research is needed to determine whether PMOS independently affects Alzheimer’s disease or dementia risk.

“I think we need to be careful about drawing conclusions too early. The research raises some good questions, but it doesn’t prove that PCOS [PMOS] causes Alzheimer’s disease,” said Dung Trinh, MD, internist, of MemorialCare Medical Group and Chief Medical Officer of Healthy Brain Clinic in Irvine, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“What it does reinforce is how important metabolic health may be when it comes to protecting our brains as we get older,” he added.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who also wasn’t involved in the study, agreed. She also added that more attention and research need to be given to PMOS, brain changes, and future risks of dementia.

There are various ways that PMOS and dementia may share pathways and overlap, according to the researchers. Some of these shared pathways include:

Trinh explained that insulin resistance may be one of the most important connections between PMOS and dementia.

Although insulin is commonly associated with diabetes and blood sugar regulation, it also plays an important role in brain function. When insulin signaling doesn’t work properly, it may interfere with how brain cells use energy, potentially contributing to problems with memory and thinking over time.

Chronic inflammation, which can occur in people with PMOS, may also play a role in Alzheimer’s disease, Trinh told Healthline.

“Researchers are looking at how these metabolic changes may affect amyloid and tau, two proteins associated with Alzheimer’s. Some brain imaging studies have even found differences in brain structure and function among women with PCOS [PMOS],” he said.

Ross added that elevated androgen levels, which are common in people with PMOS, may also play a role in dementia risk.

“An important distinction is that these risk factors are not present in every woman with PMOS, and having PMOS does not automatically mean someone will experience cognitive decline,” cautioned Garcia.

Garcia noted that many of the dementia risk factors associated with PMOS are modifiable.

“Regular exercise, including both cardiovascular activity and strength training, can improve insulin sensitivity, help with weight management, and support cardiovascular and brain health,” she added.

“A Mediterranean-style diet, with plenty of vegetables, fruits, whole grains, healthy fats, and lean sources of protein, is a reasonable place to start,” he said.

Managing blood sugar, cholesterol, and blood pressure is also important, Trinh and Garcia noted.

“Medication, like metformin, can also improve insulin resistance, which may further reduce the risk of dementia,” Ross added.

Getting adequate sleep, avoiding smoking, and staying mentally and socially active are additional ways to support long-term brain health, Garcia told Healthline.

“For someone with PCOS [PMOS], I would encourage regular visits with their healthcare provider to monitor metabolic health and address problems early,” said Trinh.

“While we cannot say that these interventions specifically prevent dementia in women with PMOS, we know they benefit overall metabolic and cardiovascular health, which are closely connected to brain health,” explained Garcia.
