#4790. Cancer Taught Dolph Lundgren He’s Not Invincible. Now He’s Finding New Strength.

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

After three years with no evidence of disease, the action legend is training smarter—and living differently.

DOLPH LUNDGREN HAS had one hell of a life. From being plucked from obscurity into a modeling career after studying chemical engineering at MIT, to dating Grace Jones, to becoming one of the iconic bad guys of the 1980s, what hasn’t he done? Just one of those things would be a highlight in anybody’s life. But Dolph Lundgren isn’t just anybody.

Seemingly cut from stone and delivered to America ready-made to star in films, his path upon arrival from Sweden wasn’t always easy. In the new documentary, Dolph: Unbreakable, Lundgren gets candid about a childhood of abuse and the struggle to put that behind him. He also discusses the films he felt didn’t meet his standards after he was established as a household name thanks to roles in Rocky IV, Universal Soldier, and Masters of the Universe. While there are certainly gems to be discovered in that direct-to-video period, it's fascinating to watch the man many know as Ivan Drago, a brute with few words, open up about his life and career. Perhaps the film’s biggest revelation is that of Lundgren’s fight with cancer, a diagnosis that, at one point, gave him just a few months to live.

That fight scaffolds Dolph: Unbreakable, and it’s moving to watch a man so seemingly superhuman allow himself to be so vulnerable. Now, on the other side of that battle and going strong, Lundgren is out in the world touring with his new memoir, Fights Worth Fighting: Finding Strength in Struggle, alongside the doc. Taking a moment from his busy schedule, the 69-year-old legend sat down with Men’s Health to discuss his new fitness app, Brandon Lee and learning from Sylvester Stallone.

MEN’S HEALTH: How’s your health these days?

DOLPH LUNDGREN: It's good, man. It's good. I've been NED—no evidence of disease—for three years now. I'm doing a scan every couple of months. I mean, I still work out. I work out a lot now, actually, like I used to. I’m feeling great. I'm working on a fitness app—My friend Arnold has one. I'm going to do a much smaller personal one about exactly how I work out; It's more confined to what I do.

But physically, I feel good. Psychologically, once you have the cancer diagnosis, you're always wondering what's going to come in the future, but it keeps you honest on some level. It keeps me honest about enjoying the moments.

MH: Even in the scariest moments of your diagnosis in the documentary, you always looked like you were in great shape. How has your approach to fitness evolved as you’ve gotten older?

DL: It's gotten a little more focused. As you get older, you have more responsibilities and you have less time, especially these days with all the digital noise in the world. I think I’ve also gotten a little smarter. The cancer journey made me realize I'm not invincible, and even though I want to do crazy stuff like I used to and spar with 25-year-olds and run up the mountain, I can’t do that anymore.

I said, "No, I'm going to cut back on the crazy stuff." And I've devised this workout schedule that's based on 30- to 40-minute workouts a couple times a week, and I've distilled it down to what I think really works, what doesn't get you injured, and what you have access to. Most people have access to a gym. So, most of it is strength training. There's some cardio involved, plus a little movement and mobility from martial arts. I've come up with a pretty clever and pretty efficient program.

MH: I love how candid you get in the film, especially about your own work. You’re hard on some of your direct-to-video work, but those projects still have a lot of fans. Is there anything you think went under the radar?

DL: Look, what I would say is I'm proud of my own work, but I may not be totally ecstatic about how the films turned out sometimes. I wasn't the director. Some of the movies, however, like Command Performance, I'm very proud of. That's a movie I directed. I think what I said in the doc was that the focus wasn’t necessarily to make a good movie. It was just to make quick money. I definitely feel good about the movies I directed. I feel good about Command Performance and Wanted Man. Movies like I Come in Peace—I know a lot of people like that one. Unfortunately, we couldn’t include that one in the documentary. There’s only so much space. [Laughs] They're all testaments of their time. They may not be prominent, but they've clearly played a part in my life and my development as a person and as an actor.

MH: Showdown in Little Tokyo is an all-time favorite of mine. I love your dynamic in it with Brandon Lee. What are your memories of him?

DL: My main memory of him is that he was a great guy. We really got along very well, both off-screen and on-screen. Obviously, I was a fan of his dad's, Bruce. I think his mom, Linda Lee, was half Swedish. I think her grandmother was from Sweden. He had been to Sweden, and had a quarter of Scandinavian descent. That's why he was tall, and had those good looks—that mix between her and Bruce.

He spoke some Swedish, and we bonded over that. Then, of course, the martial arts: he did the same style as his dad, and I was doing Kyokushin karate, a different style. We had such a great time together. I was very, very upset when I got that call a couple years later that he'd gotten killed in some freak accident. He would've certainly been a huge star.

MH: You were speaking earlier about your development as an actor. You’ve always been a compelling screen presence, but you’ve become better and better as you’ve gotten older. You give incredible performances in movies like Creed II and Universal Soldier: Day of Reckoning. What’s it been like to stretch yourself?

DL: It's been great. I remember an interview with Russell Crowe where he was asked, "How do you create a great character?" And he says, "Work with a great director." It's hard to display great acting if you're not working with a great director, because he's the artist. That's why Marlon Brando made bad movies once in a while. He was usually interesting, but maybe the movie was forgettable.

As a martial artist, as an engineer, I was used to being trained from the ground up properly for years. Martial arts took seven years to get a black belt. I started acting when I was 23, and I was thrown into a big movie very quickly. The movie was a hit, and suddenly I'm in Hollywood. I'm now starring in my own movies, but I didn't have much experience. I had to learn on the job, and it wasn't easy. But think about Stallone, for instance. He’d done some great acting, but before that, he was a writer. He wanted to be a star early on. I hadn't even thought of it before Rocky IV. It took me years after that to acquire more confidence and skill.

With recent films, especially Creed II and Aquaman, I had a chance to work with better directors and actors, and play more interesting characters. I still do action stuff and action comedies where it's not as focused, but I do like to apply myself. Now, I'm interested in applying myself, post-cancer, to dramatic roles to see what happens, because I haven't done it yet. It's going to be interesting. I'm doing some of those kinds of movies this year and next year.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

#4789. GM is recalling more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs over a brake software defect

General Motors (GM) issued a recall affecting more than 67,000 Cadillac and Chevy EVs because a software glitch can cause a temporary loss of braking.

The recall comes after a 2024 Cadillac Lyriq ran into a garage (at a low speed). On April 10, 2026, a GM tech expert submitted a report to GM’s Speak Up for Safety (SUFS) program for review.

After internal testing, GM was able to replicate the glitch, similar to a recall it issued in 2024. GM said the issue stems from a software glitch with the brake system control module (BSCM) that can cause a temporary loss of braking while driving under certain conditions.

When drivers lightly tap the brakes during a sharp turn and the vehicle hits a bump, the software’s slip calculation may misinterpret wheel movement.

In some instances, it can lead to a temporary loss of braking. The glitch only affects pAWD vehicles, including certain Cadillac Lyriq, Celestiq, Vistiq, and Chevy Blazer EV.

In a letter sent to the NHTSA on October 29, GM said the recall impacted 67,380 vehicles total, including certain:

According to documents filed with the NHTSA, GM found 24 field complaints related to the issue. Of these, 20 involved minor accidents, and two involved allegations of minor injuries.

The complaints were received between February 24, 2024, and June 11, 2026. GM said it has implemented software corrections in production over the past few months.

GM will update the BSCM software via an over-the-air (OTA) update or through a dealer, free of charge.

Owner notification letters are expected to be mailed out on December 14, 2026. In the meantime, you can contact Cadillac’s customer service at 1-800-333-4223 or Chevrolet’s customer service at 1-800-222-1020. GM’s recall number is N262570900.

You can also contact the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration Hotline at 1-888-327-4236 or visit the nhtsa.gov website for more information. The NHTSA campaign number is 26V717.

#4788. Later Daters Still Love Sex

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

Among many destructive, ageist stereotypes prevalent in America, one of the most pervasive is that older adults aren’t interested in, capable of, or engaged in having sex. On the contrary, research shows that about three-quarters of those aged 57-64, over half of those aged 65-74, and a quarter of those aged 75-85 had sexual contact with someone in the past year. And this doesn’t even count those who would have chosen to have sex but had no opportunity.

While the stereotypes are alive and well regarding the nability of older adults to have sex, many, if not most, either do have, or are interested in having, sexual activity with a partner. It’s true older adults may struggle with aspects of sex they didn’t confront when younger—men with the ability to maintain erections or ejaculate; women with lubrication or discomfort. But there are excellent treatments for these conditions, and humans are creative. Older adults engage in satisfying romantic relationships without sexual activity, satisfying sexual relationships without romance, and everything in between. And in terms of sex, older couples not only enjoy intercourse, but also non-penetrative sexual activities like hugging, cuddling, sleeping naked; manual, masturbatory, and oral play activities, and more.

A recent study by Harris and Melanson (2026) interviewed 100 single older adults aged 60-83 (50 women and 50 men) recruited from dating sites for gender, racial, and educational diversity. More older adults are single today than ever before (due to longer lives and the acceptance of divorce), and this group is understudied compared to older adults with partners. The Harris and Melanson study was limited by heterosexual participants, but we can extrapolate many of its findings to all relationships:

Sex is a healthy part of life throughout adulthood, whether one is single, partnered, or in between. How it looks and when it happens may change, and some adults may do well without a partner, but the majority of older adults, like younger adults, find partnered sex an important ingredient of healthy social lives, life satisfaction, and wellbeing.

Harris and Melanson surveyed an often-ignored group of older adults—those who are single. Because they found them through dating sites, we know participants in the sample were at least somewhat interested in pursuing romantic and/or sexual partnerships. It’s up to future researchers to explore whether single older adults not interested in dating are equally interested in sex (with another person), or simply feel content alone; as well as how these results may be different in LGBTQ+ and other marginalized populations.

Harris, L., & Melanson, C. (2026). “The Shop Is Not Closed”: Sex and Sexuality Among Older Adult Daters. The Journal of Sex Research, 1–13. https://doi.org/10.1080/00224499.2026.2614315

#4787. Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

“Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

In June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”

The fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a big topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

We also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

Many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

The line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She says her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

“I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

But despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

“I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

“There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”

Ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”

It’s important to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

Stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

One of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

#4786. First: Volvo CE Electric equipment does the work, without disturbing the wildlife

For the first time, electric equipment assets are being put to work in the National Wildlife Refuge System, where a battery-powered, zero-emission ECR25 Electric compact excavator and L25 Electric compact wheel loader made by Volvo CE are making the wild more accessible to everyone.

Construction work isn’t exactly welcome in the wilderness – between diesel exhaust, engine noises, and the constant rumble of heavy machinery, even a relatively small project can have a big impact on the native wildlife. To minimize that impact, US Fish and Wildlife Service is turning to Volvo CE and its compact excavators and wheel loaders to get the job done, building out a new, ADA accessible trail in Virginia’s Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge.

“We are excited to partner with the US Fish and Wildlife Service on this project to demonstrate Volvo’s commitment to lowering emissions and working to build the future we all want and need,” said Dr. Ray Gallant, VP of Product Management and Productivity, Volvo CE. “Projects like the one at the Occoquan Bay National Wildlife Refuge give a glimpse of how electric machines can create a more climate-friendly future for the construction industry.”

The refuge is home to a diverse array of grasslands, wetlands, and woods that attract red foxes, painted turtles, osprey, river otters, and countless other rarely seen species – and the ADA accessible path being laid down by the L25 Electric compact wheel loader will allow wheelchair-bound visitors to travel a half-mile-long trail around one of the pond. Meanwhile, the ECR25 Electric compact excavator will be digging trenches to improve drainage from the pond and helping to place a viewing platform that extends out over the water.

Keeping the machines running is a portable EV ARC solar-powered charging system from Beam Global that’s designed to drive down the project’s carbon footprint even further.

#4785. I’ll Be 72 When My Youngest Kid Graduates High School. I Wouldn’t Have it Any Other Way.

“I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can,” says comedian Andy Richter.

I DON’T CONSIDER myself to be very “Hollywood,” but in terms of fatherhood, I’m practically a cliché.

It’s because I had my kids in waves. There’s my son Will, 26, and daughter Mercy, 21, from my first marriage, and my daughter Cornelia, 6, from my second and present marriage.

There are a lot of us old-dads-of-young-kids out here, and the main reason is that there are so many Los Angeles men who, after they get that first marriage out of the way, employ a sort of Benjamin Button philosophy towards the subsequent ones in that as time marches forward and the end of life moves closer, the wives get younger and younger.

I don’t lump myself in with those geezers, though, because I am 60 and my wife is 50, and the narrowness of that merely ten-year gap affords me the moral superiority of a guy married to someone with whom he can have actual conversations.

But the fact remains that I was 54 when my youngest was born. And yes, I have done all the math. I’ll be 72 when she graduates high school, 76 when she graduates college, and god knows what kind of drooling diapered mess I’ll be when I’m giving the toast at her wedding, champagne flute in one hand, the other one white-knuckling my walker.

But it is what it is. I fell in love with a single mother who, after many years of a successful career, wanted a child and hadn’t found a suitable partner to raise one with. A relationship with Jen was always going to be a package deal, and it’s the best one I’ve ever been lucky enough to gladly tumble head over heels into.

When I started letting people know that we were engaged and that I was going to adopt the then-two-year-old Cornelia (I was calling it “getting back into the toddler business”), people had one of two reactions.

The first was along the lines of Why the fuck would you do that? For so many people, and especially parents, the idea of going back to raising a pre-pre-schooler was incomprehensible. To them it was like driving through a hurricane and then making a U-ey to take one more crack at it for fun.

The other reaction was that I was some kind of saint. That to so selflessly dive back into the stress of making a person out of what is basically a little wild animal that can delete seven phone apps in less than one minute made me some sort of super dad, the menschiest of mensches.

This take was, while flattering, a little embarrassing, because years ago I figured out that all you have to do be hoisted on metaphorical shoulders and pronounced a Good Dad is about 30 percent of the work that it takes to be a Good Mom.

I also felt a little sheepish about the idea that signing up to help raise a two year old was somehow heroic because I knew that this little girl was giving me a gift: approximately 16 years of not having to figure out was I was going to do with myself.

“What should I do now?” has been a question that has plagued me for my entire life in both the micro and the macro. It’s why I smoked for almost 20 years. When you’re raising a child, you don’t have to come up with something to do—you’ve got that kid to take care of. You want a purpose? How about making a decent human?

When you are raising a child, it’s always good work. You are never wasting your time on an unworthy project. (A quick stroll through my IMDB page will show that I have done that more than a few times.)

So when a group of kindergarten girls asks me, “Are you Cornelia’s grandpa?” I just let it roll off my back, because they don’t know about the scam I’m running. I have found a way to get to do the thing I love most for as long as I possibly can.

And there’s a good chance that by the time she’s ready to head out on her own, her older brother and sister might start having children, which means I will possibly get to have a life filled with babies and little kids for a long, long time. And that is a huge win for me.

I once heard Bob Odenkirk say on a podcast, “When you’re raising little kids, you know what your job is.” I know exactly what he means, and I love my job.

Andy Richter, author of Elf Unwrapped, is a Los Angeles–based comedian, actor, writer, and host best known as Conan O’Brien’s longtime sidekick, who also hosts the Three Questions podcast and The Andy Richter Call-In Show and had a longer-than-expected run on Dancing with the Stars.

#4784. Getting More Physical Activity May Help With Your Perimenopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

A new study found that exercising more frequently may help alleviate perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes, anxiety, and urinary issues.

The study results were recently presented at The Menopause Society’s 2026 Annual Conference.

Perimenopause is the transitional period leading up to menopause.

Due to hormonal changes that mark the end of a person’s reproductive years, symptoms like hot flashes, mood swings, brain fog, insomnia, and urinary incontinence are common.

Past studies show that lifestyle modifications, such as eating a healthy diet, managing stress, and getting enough physical activity, can help reduce some perimenopause symptoms.

“Physical activity is low cost, accessible, and already known to benefit sleep, mood, and heart and bone health — all areas that matter a great deal during perimenopause,” said study lead and co-author Liudmila Zhaunova, PhD, director of science at Flo Health — the developer of a women’s health tracking app, which was used to collect health data for this study. “But when we looked at the research, there was surprisingly little evidence specific to perimenopause.”

“Hormone therapy isn’t suitable or desired for everyone, so women deserve a broader set of evidence-based options,” Zhaunova told Healthline. “The more we understand about accessible, lifestyle-based approaches, the better equipped women and their healthcare providers are to build a plan that works for them.”

Study researchers recruited more than 1,800 women from around the globe who were using the Flo app.

Study participants were asked to complete online surveys about their physical activity, from not being physically active to exercising more than 5 days a week.

Participants were also asked to report on their perimenopause symptoms in three categories — somatic (body-based issues like hot flashes), psychological (mental health issues like mood changes), and urogenital (issues regarding the urinary or vaginal areas). Researchers rated the severity of these symptoms using the Menopause Rating Scale (MRS).

The researchers found that higher rates of physical activity were associated with fewer perimenopausal symptoms across all three categories.

“Perimenopause symptoms are wide-ranging, and women often experience several at once,” Zhaunova said. “Seeing a lower symptom burden across all three domains suggests that being more active may be relevant to women’s overall experience, not just one symptom.”

Additionally, the scientists discovered that the greatest exercise benefit was observed in the reduction of perimenopausal psychological symptoms.

“Psychological symptoms, such as low mood, irritability, anxiety, and exhaustion, are among the most disruptive parts of perimenopause, and they’re often overlooked or not recognized as related to this life stage,” Zhaunova explained.

“Our findings suggest that physical activity may matter most for mood and anxiety-related symptoms,” she continued.

“This could help women and clinicians have more informed conversations about how to support mental well-being during perimenopause. That said, women with more symptoms may find it harder to exercise, so we need further research to understand the direction of the relationship.”

Sherry Ross, MD, a board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, said that regular exercise could potentially help relieve perimenopause symptoms like hot flashes and mood changes. Ross wasn’t involved in this study, but noted other benefits of exercising during this life stage:

“Exercise releases endorphins, improves blood vessel health, lowers inflammation, helps reset circadian rhythm, and improves the body’s internal cooling system,” Ross told Healthline. “Collectively, these changes ease anxiety, irritability, mood changes, sleep, and fatigue.”

“There were mixed reviews on how exercise benefits hot flashes, but exercise does help with weight control, which may benefit hot flashes,” she said. “Strengthening the pelvic floor and core may help with the urinary symptoms women many experience in perimenopause.”

Prudence Hall, MD, an OB-GYN in private practice in Santa Monica, CA, and author of “Radiant Again & Forever,” said that building a sustainable exercise routine requires consistency, joy, and community. Hall wasn’t involved in the study, but shared some exercise tips for perimenopausal women.

“Too often in midlife, previously stable women suddenly plummet into deep depression and anxiety, only to be prescribed multiple medications with debilitating side effects that never address the underlying biology,” Hall said.

“While hormone optimization remains essential to correct these endocrine deficiencies, exercise serves as a powerful, non-pharmaceutical therapy that directly targets the true root causes by revitalizing our cellular health and restoring overall vitality.”

#4783. Inside the World of an Intimacy Coordinator

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Recently, after seeing a stage play, I spoke to a lead actor about how she is able to feel safe during physically intimate scenes in front of an audience. She told me that there is an intimacy coordinator who comes onto the set to make sure the actors’ feelings about intimacy with other actors are taken into account. She has also worked on film sets with an intimacy coordinator when she felt uneasy and vulnerable in front of the camera and crew and her lover in the film.

I wanted to find out more about this and, unexpectedly, I met intimacy coordinator Christina McHugh at an event in New Mexico a few weeks later. I asked her to define what it is that she does when she is hired to work on films. “Old-fashioned doctors went house to house, a mail person goes door to door, and an intimacy coordinator goes set to set.” The geographical areas she covered were Albuquerque, Santa Fe, and movie ranches. She goes from one set to another.

She explained that making actors feel psychologically and physically safe was mostly prep work, before the scenes were shot. She had extensive conversations with directors and then worked with the actors to find out what their boundaries were and to get their consent. “Then I would go back to the director and impart information like the fact that the actor wanted less nudity. I would ask the director if it could be filmed a different way.”

For filming sex scenes, she used things like a “half-deflated Pilates ball to put between the actors’ crotches. There were often three layers of barriers between the actors for simulated sex. If the woman is on top of the man, her bouncing is done with a 9-inch Pilates ball that makes it look like simulated sex.”

McHugh said that her job entails negotiating boundaries with individual actors, the director, and trying to get all sides to agree. This is especially true in building trust on the set of a film with hyper-exposure, that includes nudity, simulated sex, and sexual violence.

Some of the sets she worked on include "Better Call Saul," "Pluribus," "Love Lies Bleeding," "Obliterated," "Duster," "The Cleaning Lady," "Waco," and "Dead for a Dollar."

I inquired where she learned her profession, and she replied that she trained with the Intimacy Professionals Association. “In about 2017, it was the first time it showed up in a credit line. It started with an HBO series, "The Deuce," which was about the porn industry. The actress felt she was being treated as a porn star and not an actress.”

I believed her when McHugh said you need a spine made of titanium to deal with producers and directors. She is not flippant about the issues actors have when she is negotiating with them. She said that young female actors tell her about being victims of sexual predation, and she takes care of them. This is an important part of her job, which she takes very seriously.

Entertainment writer Liz Konkel had this to say in a recent post on Cinema Blend: “The rules have certainly changed in regard to how sex scenes are filmed, thanks to the rise of intimacy coordinators on sets. Now, this doesn't mean we don't get plenty of steamy content. However, what it does mean is that more technical work goes into creating such scenes. In a post #MeToo Movement industry, these coordinators also help ensure actors feel comfortable and protected during intimate scenes.”

In the same article, she also addressed how actors’ boundaries and trust concerns were dealt with before intimacy coordinators. “Back in the early aughts, scenes were seemingly required of the actors if it was in the script. However, some performers have since shared stories where trust was taken advantage of on set. For instance, "Basic Instinct’s" Sharon Stone has made claims involving inappropriate requests for nudity amid production. With that, many now consider intimacy coordinators to be essential.”

#4782. High gas prices are pumping up used EV sales: these are FLYING off the lot

A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices are driving an unprecedented number of used car buyers to consider going electric, and that increased demand without a corresponding increase in supply means these used EVs are flying off dealer lots.

Days on the lot. That’s dealer-speak for the average number of days a given vehicle typically sits in inventory before finding a buyer. That’s critically important to dealers, since the vehicles on their lots are commonly financed through something called floorplan credit, and every additional day a car spends on a dealer’s lot can mean another day of interest payments and another day closer to a curtailment. Days on the lot can be even more important to dealers when it comes to cars owned outright, as well, as the dealers can have significant cash tied up in vehicles they’ve purchased outright, and every day those cars sit is another day that money isn’t working for them elsewhere.

That’s what makes this month’s fastest-selling used EVs particularly interesting, because these used EVs aren’t just selling fast for electric vehicles – they’re selling fast, period.

Dealer news sources Automotive News and Cox Automotive report that the average new car spent 82 days on the lot in October, with a 75-day target being an industry-wide benchmark. At the same time, the Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron Quattro with its 258-mile EPA-estimated range is turning in just 29.8 days. (!)

That Audi’s not alone. In a recently-released vehicle pricing study, iSeeCars reported that the Toyota BZ4x, Lexus RZ300e, Honda Prologue, and Borrás-family favorite Polestar 2 are all turning in an average of 35 days or less, with the BMW i4, iX, Kia EV6, and Chevrolet Equinox EV just a day or two behind.

“The results reveal a market where EVs are appreciating in average asking price much faster than other drivetrains, while also spending less time waiting for buyers,” said iSeeCars Executive Analyst Karl Brauer, who found that average transaction prices for EVs rose 9.8% last month as ICE-powered vehicles stayed steady, rising just 0.3%. “Hybrids are experiencing moderate improvements in price and selling speed, while gasoline-powered vehicles have seen their selling times increase,” he adds, “despite relatively stable prices.”

@Jo Borras , you forgot to mention about one more factor (besides: "A new car affordability crisis and punishing gas prices..."). Back in September last year there was still electric vehicle tax credits in the United States that has ended on September 30, 2025.

Used electric vehicles averaged a price of $32,533 in September 2026, up $2,896 from the $29,637 ATP recorded a year earlier.

#4780. BLUETTI’s flexible $1,099 Apex 200 backs up your home – and powers your RV

What do you actually need to keep running when the power goes out? For most households, the fridge, wifi, phones, and a few other essentials come first. Buying enough battery storage for every appliance in the house can come later – and that’s the appeal of BLUETTI’s latest launch, the Apex 200 portable power station.

The Apex 200 starts with 2.56kWh of storage and 3.2kW of continuous AC output, with the option to add batteries when you need longer backup. Built-in RV connections also mean it can earn its keep between blackouts.

BLUETTI launches the Apex 200 on November 4, with standalone super early-bird pricing starting at $1,099 through November 18. Electrek readers can get an extra 5% off with code ELECTREK5OFF.

Here’s how to work out which setup is worth buying for your home or RV.

The Apex 200 takes the expandable design of BLUETTI’s flagship Apex series and puts it in a smaller package.

You get a 2,560Wh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery. The 3.2kW of continuous AC output increases to 3.6kW when an expansion battery is connected or the unit is actively charging.

The enclosure holds all that in 36.2 liters and weighs 26.9kg (59.3 lb). You’ll want two hands to move it, but it’s convenient to move it between home and your camper.

BLUETTI’s UltraCell technology delivers an industry-leading energy density of 70.7 Wh/L, yet the Apex 200 is more than 50% smaller by volume than class competitors. For an RV owner, that smaller footprint frees up room for other gear.

There’s also a tilted display and four app-controllable AC outlets. That might not sound like a big deal, but when the battery is on the floor or under your desk and you want to check or redirect its charge, it means you don’t have to crouch.

BLUETTI calls its approach “Start Small. Scale Big. Power More.” BLUETTI says Apex 300 users reported liking the modular design but wanted something easier to handle day to day. The Apex 200 offers them a lower entry point, with room to add capacity rather than replace the main unit.

Before buying a portable power station, you’ll want to know how much power your appliances draw and how much energy they use over time.

For example, a 150W appliance running continuously for 10 hours uses 1,500Wh. A 1,500W appliance gets through that same amount in one hour. Running a coffee maker briefly is a different proposition from keeping a high-draw appliance on all afternoon.

A rough runtime calculation is: Usable battery capacity in watt-hours ÷ average load in watts = hours of operation.

Divide the Apex 200’s nominal 2,560Wh by a steady 150W load, and you get about 17 hours before accounting for conversion losses and the battery system’s own power use. Real runtime will be lower.

Refrigerators complicate that calculation because their compressors cycle on and off. Check measured daily energy use where possible, along with startup demand – motors can briefly draw more power when they kick on.

If your usual blackout lasts four to 12 hours, start by looking at the Apex 200 on its own.

BLUETTI estimates it can run a 150W refrigerator for 10–12 hours, or support low-draw essentials such as CPAPs, wifi routers, and mobile devices for two to three days, depending on the equipment and how it’s used. That doesn’t mean every device on that list will run together for three days. Your combined load determines the runtime.

The Apex 200 also gives you more control over where that energy goes. Four independently controllable Smart AC outlets built right into the unit – no need to buy smart plugs! – let you switch individual devices on and off through the BLUETTI App, set schedules, and apply state-of-charge controls. So if something doesn’t need power overnight, you can turn off its power at the outlet and save the fridge’s battery.

BLUETTI calls the feature an industry first for portable power stations. The system also works with Amazon Alexa, Google Home, and Home Assistant.

A UPS function switches connected equipment to battery power in 15 milliseconds. Check that switching time against your equipment’s requirements, especially for a CPAP or other sensitive device.

With AC output on and the display off, idle consumption drops to just 10.5W.

A winter freeze or severe storm can leave you without grid power for days. That’s when adding extra storage starts to make more sense.

For typical power outages, adding one or two BLUETTI B300K batteries can extend essential home backup to two to three days.

But you can go further. One Apex 200 supports up to six B500K expansion batteries, bringing its maximum capacity to 33.28kWh.

But a bigger battery still needs recharging eventually. The Apex 200 accepts up to 3kW of solar input across two independent channels:

With a correctly configured array of SORA 500 portable solar panels making full use of those inputs, BLUETTI says the base battery can charge from 0 to 80% in 50 minutes, or reach 100% in 1.7 hours using solar alone.

A solar generator setup lets you recharge during daylight. The Apex 200 can also be charged with wall AC, vehicle charging, and compatible gas-generator charging. A suitable 30A generator connection can help replenish the battery when solar production falls short.

The Apex 200 can also form part of a larger home battery backup system through BLUETTI’s Hub A1 parallel box.

BLUETTI specifies up to 6kW of continuous AC output and approximately 100kWh of storage across a parallel system using up to three Apex 200 units.

That’s a significant increase over the standalone battery, but your daily consumption still matters. A steady 1kW load uses 24kWh in 24 hours. Heavy-draw appliances can make a large battery feel much smaller.

BLUETTI positions its larger configurations for three to four days of essential-panel backup. How close you get depends on your batteries, appliances, and ability to recharge.

If you want automatic backup through your home’s electrical panel, confirm the compatible transfer equipment, supported circuits, voltage, and output for the exact bundle. Those details determine what you can actually keep running.

Start with your most likely outage, then decide whether you need more runtime, a charging source, or both.

Extra batteries extend runtime. Solar panels or another charging source recharge them. For outages that stretch into days, both can be worth having.

When shopping for a camper van or travel trailer, choosing a battery comes down to more than just capacity. Among its 10 output ports are two connections RV owners will appreciate having built in.

The native 30A TT-30R RV outlet plugs directly into travel trailer shore power inlets for 120V power.

The 12V/30A Anderson port can directly power compatible DC equipment, including portable fridges and communications gear. This avoids converting battery power to AC and then back to DC, cutting out unnecessary conversion steps.

For charging between campsites, the system can pair with the BLUETTI Charger 2, which combines alternator and solar charging support. It lets you use driving time to replenish the battery through faster vehicle alternator charging, then use solar when you’re parked.

BLUETTI’s recommended mobile bundle is the Apex 200 + SORA 500 solar panel + Charger 2. You get storage for camp, solar charging during your stay, and alternator charging on the road. Compatible campground AC gives you another option.

The Apex 200 is the better fit if you value a smaller enclosure, easier transport, native RV ports, and a lower upfront cost. You can start with 2.56kWh and expand to 33.28kWh on one unit, or approximately 100kWh across a fully expanded parallel system.

The Apex 300 is worth considering if your priority is higher native output and capacity for a system that will mostly stay at home. It offers 3,840W of output and 2,764.8Wh of battery storage, and BLUETTI positions it for more advanced home backup, including compatible 120V/240V configurations.

For someone who wants a battery for both blackouts and RV trips, the Apex 200’s size and connections make a useful combination. You can buy the storage you need now and add more when your power needs change.

The Apex 200 launches November 4, with the standalone unit starting at $1,099 during the November 4–18 super early-bird promotion.

Founded in 2013, BLUETTI allows millions of users across more than 120 countries to stay safe and prepared. Its in-house R&D supports a range of solar generators and home backup systems for outage preparation, RV travel, and off-grid living and recreation.

Shop the Apex 200 and launch bundles, and use ELECTREK5OFF at checkout for an extra 5% savings.

#4779. Aniioki A9 Pro Max review: Basically an electric motorcycle that you can pedal

There are electric bikes, there are electric motorcycles, and then there are machines like the Aniioki A9 Pro Max that plant a flag somewhere in the increasingly large no-man’s-land between the two.

Technically, it has pedals. You can pedal it fairly effectively too, with the actually adjustable seat. You can even pedal it for fun, which is more than I can say for some of the increasingly motorcycle-shaped “e-bikes” I’ve tested lately.

But let’s get something out of the way right at the beginning: this isn’t a street-legal electric bicycle in the US. Not when we’re talking about dual motors producing up to 6,000W of peak power and speeds of around 45 mph.

And you know what? That’s fine. As long as we’re all honest about what this thing is.

The Aniioki A9 Pro Max is absolutely massive, and the spec sheet makes that abundantly clear.

The version I tested uses a pair of 2,500W direct-drive hub motors, one in each wheel, with Aniioki claiming 3,000W peak power from each motor. That gives the bike a combined peak figure of 6,000W and up to 250 Nm of combined torque. It’s hard to overstate how massive that is.

Then there’s the battery. You can choose between a 60V 70Ah pack with 4.2 kWh of capacity or an even larger 60V 80Ah pack packing 4.8 kWh. For comparison, many typical commuter e-bikes have somewhere around 500-700 Wh of battery. The smaller battery here is roughly six to eight times that size. That’s absolutely in the territory of legit light electric motorcycles.

Aniioki claims up to 230+ miles (370 km) of pedal-assist range, though as usual, you should take maximum e-bike range figures as best-case numbers. Using the throttle and enjoying those big motors is going to dramatically reduce that figure. Even so, with more than 4 kWh of battery underneath you, range anxiety isn’t exactly the first thing that comes to mind.

All that hardware comes with a predictable penalty: weight. The 70Ah model tips the scales at around 188 lb (85 kg), while the 80Ah version approaches 193 lb (87.5 kg). Those aren’t e-bike weights. Those are motorcycle weights. Again, you can see the direction this is going.

Here’s where the A9 Pro Max gets more interesting to me.

A lot of high-powered e-motos include pedals seemingly as a regulatory fig leaf. They’re technically there, but the geometry is so bad that nobody in their right mind would want to pedal the thing farther than across a parking lot. Even some smaller and presumably Class 2 legal e-bikes that have moto-style frames are nearly unpedalable for actual riding over any reasonable distance.

But the A9 here is actually pedalable thanks to having something that more closely resembles a bicycle seat, plus adjustability that lets riders dial in the correct seat height.

The A9 Pro Max feels more like a strange combination of an oversized fat-tire e-bike and a small electric motorcycle. There’s a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain and a huge 72-tooth chainring, meaning the pedals aren’t entirely ornamental.

I actually enjoyed pedaling it with the pedal assist engaged. You’re obviously not going to mistake a nearly 200-pound machine rolling on enormous 26 x 4.8-inch tires for a lightweight fitness bike, but there’s something fun about contributing some human power while two giant hub motors do most of the heavy lifting.

And when you don’t feel like pedaling, there’s a full-twist throttle waiting for you.

That combination is really the appeal here. You can ride it more like an e-bike when the mood strikes, or twist the throttle and treat it more like a lightweight e-moto.

And again, I don’t want to beat a dead horse here, but remember: the pedals don’t make this an electric bicycle. It’s still an e-moto, but it’s one that you can actually have fun pedaling. You can treat it like a mech suit, where pedaling translates into crazy power, as if you have super-human legs. And with the insanely large 72t chainring, pedaling at higher speeds is actually doable. Though I’ll tell you right now, pedaling at 40 mph (64 km/h) is not exactly a normal or natural feeling.

And it’s worth pointing out that at a starting price of US $2,899 (or more for the larger battery capacities), that’s a fairly reasonable price compared to most e-motos that can be more limiting in how and where you can ride them.

Fortunately, Aniioki seems to understand that putting this much power on two wheels requires more serious components than the average bicycle.

The braking setup is particularly wild. There are two massive 300mm brake rotors on the front wheel and another 300mm rotor out back, along with a linked CBS braking system. The front uses custom eight-piston calipers (the pair of quad-piston calipers) while the rear gets a custom six-piston setup.

There’s also an adjustable air-suspension fork with 110mm of travel, rear suspension to smooth out bumps at higher speeds, integrated lighting and turn signals, and a large five-inch display that even incorporates features like Bluetooth audio and a recording camera.

That brings us to the elephant in the room.

In the US, consumer-product rules generally define a low-speed electric bicycle around a motor of less than 750W and a maximum motor-powered speed below 20 mph (32 km/h), while individual states use their own operating laws that typically match the familiar Class 1/2/3 framework. A 6,000W machine capable of around 45 mph (72 km/h) blows straight through normal limits.

So please don’t see pedals and assume this belongs on your local bicycle path.

Where and how you can legally operate something like the A9 Pro Max depends on your local laws and whether it can qualify under another vehicle category. For many owners, the sensible place to enjoy its full performance is going to be private property or other areas where such vehicles are permitted.

That caveat doesn’t make the bike itself bad. It just means buyers need to understand what they’re buying.

And judged on what it actually is rather than what the word “e-bike” on the product page suggests, I had a lot of fun on it.

There are certainly riders who would look at a nearly 200-pound, 45 mph machine and say, “Why not just buy an electric motorcycle?” That’s a perfectly reasonable question.

In addition to kW power limits, the legal boundary for what is an e-bike should also include weight. Anything over 100lbs including battery is no longer an e-bike and it carries a dangerous amount of momentum once it is cruising. 190 lbs is ridiculous.

But I also understand the appeal of this weird middle ground. The A9 Pro Max retains enough bicycle DNA that you can pedal it around and enjoy pedal assist, yet has enough battery and motor underneath you to deliver something much closer to small-motorcycle performance when you twist the throttle.

Imagine going off-road and getting to fly up hills while pedaling hard, but then being able to switch to throttle once your legs get worn out. Sure, it’s not everyone’s cup of tea, but it’s a cup of tea.

This bike is big. It’s heavy. It’s absurdly powerful by e-bike standards. And it absolutely isn’t the machine I’d recommend for someone looking for a normal street-legal electric bicycle.

But if what you actually want is a big, powerful electric two-wheeler that still lets you turn the pedals when the mood strikes, the Aniioki A9 Pro Max makes a surprisingly compelling argument for this increasingly bizarre category of pedal-equipped e-motos.

#4778. Making Change Happen

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

So, you realize that the way you have been going about things doesn’t work. You might not like the way you behave or your experience of relationships. You might not like the way you feel or how your emotions impact your decisions. And you know that if you don’t turn things around, you are going to keep repeating the same cycle. But people often struggle to change even when they genuinely want to.

I cringe when I hear people say “That’s just the way I am” while at the same time complaining about the state of their relationships. Some people use that statement to avoid responsibility. They believe their personality characteristics are fixed or have repeatedly failed in their efforts to foster change within themselves. So, rather than putting effort into changing themselves, many people prefer that others would simply come to their senses and accommodate them.

You can always work on changing the environment, and this is usually what people try first. They try to convince, persuade, nudge, and manipulate others… or they shut themselves off interpersonally, go into denial, or resort to blame and attack. But these efforts rarely result in lasting positive outcomes, and people stay happy only as long as the environment is cooperating.

Here is my recommended outline for lasting change and understanding why change can be so hard. I recommend taking these steps sequentially, as they build on each other in a cumulative fashion.

If you want to change yourself, you first need to consider what “self” you are referring to. Changing your entire being may seem insurmountable and lead you to give up before you even start. But many psychological theorists view the self as multifaceted. In other words, we are all groupings of associated parts, and we can use our more developed parts to help shape and coach the less developed ones that we are trying to change.

Sometimes change means de-emphasizing one previously dominant part of your personality and strengthening a part that was previously dormant.

People are often ambivalent about change and might actually get something out of maintaining their negative behaviors.

Before you lay aside your own ambivalence, let’s see what you actually get out of the behavior or experience you say you want to let go of. What will you lose if you change? What are the factors arguing against it?

Become conscious of your own resistance. Before evoking your commitment to a new course of action, it might help to first write down all of the positive things you get out of it. For example, what if you want to cut down on your drinking? Drinking might help you gain social acceptance and feel less lonely. It might help you relax and escape your anxiety and internal demons. Or it might simply help you escape boredom and give you something to do. These are all reasonable goals, and before you lay down the booze, you might want to consider how you are going to meet them.

But then you must ask yourself, what would need to change first before the behavior can change? Problematic behaviors are often not consciously chosen but, rather, come about through how we regulate our emotions— for example, putting too much pressure on an ambivalent romantic partner, talking too much about your insecurities, or getting aggravated and shutting down when interactions with a relationship partner get touchy.

In these examples, the root cause is often difficulty controlling your emotions.

Sometimes, your rational brain knows what it wants to do, but your emotional brain just won’t cooperate.

You should learn about how people with your personality style regulate anxiety. For example, a person with an avoidant attachment style will most likely regulate anxiety by withdrawing, shutting down, or dominating. A person with an anxious attachment style is most likely to regulate emotions by pressing too hard for reassurance or oversharing.

Learn about your personality and attachment style… then you will have an easier time changing your behavior. In other words, your conscious brain will understand what your emotional brain is doing and how to keep it from taking over.

Sometimes you just need an attitude adjustment. In the preceding paragraphs, I outlined how subconscious processes, like regulating emotions, influence behavior. But sometimes, behavior comes from the more conscious parts of your mind. In other words, your emotions follow your thoughts instead of the other way around. Attitudes are consciously held statements that you tell yourself about the way things are. You can change your attitudes by watching your self-talk and what you say to yourself in your head. Don’t expect to have angry, intolerant thoughts and be able to pull off controlling your emotions and acting loving.

If you want to change a part of yourself, it often helps to have another part supervise the process and give you supportive feedback. Take the example of inner child work. I’ve spoken about this previously in my posts. Although I’m not specifically recommending it here, it serves as a case in point.

In this approach, you learn to view your less mature, emotional, or wounded aspects of self as the child you once were. Often, that child will have gone through some difficult times that forced him/her to learn to regulate emotions and view the world in ways that don’t serve you well in adulthood. To heal this part of ourselves, we practice seeing it as a separate entity (child). The rational/adult part of our brain then gets to serve as the caring and supportive adult caregiver who can contain and advise the more emotional and less controlled part.

Sometimes when you make positive changes, the immediate result might seem negative. For example, if you quit drinking, all of your drinking buddies might get uncomfortable hanging out with you. In short, you might lose access to your old social support system and access to romantic partners if you are single. Addressing the social support issue is one of the main reasons people consider 12-step meetings. In this case, even though the short-term impact of not drinking could seem negative, the long-term impact is likely to be healthier friends and a more sustainable, healthy lifestyle.

Similarly, if you change some of your behaviors within your family system, like caretaking others, controlling, or being in the problem or “sick role,” the short-term outcome might not feel positive. Families (and work/friend systems) usually are in some sort of emotional balance (called homeostasis). When one person changes their role in the system, it throws the system out of balance, and everyone else has to adjust their behaviors or roles to accommodate the change. Some people in the system might not like the change or the disequilibrium it creates, and they may act out in an attempt to pull you back into your role. So, the short-term impact might be to feel more cut off or alienated from family members, but the long-term impact might be healthier long-term relationships that work for you.

To summarize: The suggestions I put forward in this post just touch the surface of what really would encompass a book. But I believe these are some of the most actionable principles available to get you started. And, above all, be sure to give yourself some grace and self-compassion… and this alone will do wonders to help you make change happen.

McConnell, A. R. (2011). The multiple self-aspects framework: Self-concept representation and its implications. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 15(1), 3–27.

#4777. 10 Best Colognes for Men in 2026, According to a Grooming Editor

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Plus, everything you need to know to find the fragrance that suits your unique style.

FRAGRANCE IS A deeply personal choice. Unlike moisturizers or razors, you don’t have to worry about skin type or sensitivity—cologne is all about preference. For me, I lean woody and amber year-round; however, I’ll branch out to fresher scents during the summer and spring. Whether you’ve worn the same scent for years or switch it up like socks, there’s no shortage of options to explore.

I’ve long been obsessed with Tom Ford’s bold, sophisticated Fucking Fabulous scent, so when I heard a higher-concentrated parfum was dropping earlier this year, I was stoked. It didn’t disappoint either, more than earning its name. Like the original, it layers rich tobacco and warm tonka bean into a scent that’s decadent, intoxicating, and impossible to forget. This new version amps up the intensity and staying power without ever crossing into overpowering territory.

I love how this scent hits—deep leather and roasted tonka wrapped in warm balsamic depth. The first spray bursts with fresh clary sage and lavender before melting into creamy almond and earthy orris. As it settles, the leather gets bolder, stitched with cashmere for a smooth finish. It’s unapologetic, addictive, and every bit as bold as its name. It could also double as the longest-lasting fragrance on this list.

This scent lingers for a long time, even by parfum standards. I’ve had days where I give myself a couple of sprays before leaving my apartment in the morning around 7 AM, and I can still smell it when I get home close to 7 PM. That’s nearly 12 hours of staying power.

Margiela’s Replica fragrances are designed to capture a vibe, and this one is no exception. The infusion of oud wood, leather, smoke, and crackling black pepper instantly transports you to sitting around a crackling fire, the sky ablaze with stars above you. It’s deep and layered, the type of cologne that invites people to get closer to you, and the inclusion of oud adds an air of masculine sophistication that makes it an ideal date night cologne. Compared to other oud-forward scents, this one is both identifiable as oud (i.e., elegant and sexy) but isn’t so overpowering that it’s going to leave a scent trail wherever you go.

A lot is written about Dior Sauvage, and rightfully so—it’s a dark, spicy scent that leaves a serious impression. But much of that hype overshadows the best, most masculine Dior scent: Homme. Dior Homme Parfum takes the classic scent I love and gives it a bolder, woodsy, amber twist that’s built for this chilly weather. The iris at its core feels smooth and modern—soft yet strong—balanced by warm, ambery woods that linger long after the first spray. It hits harder and lasts longer than the original Homme without losing that signature sophistication. Even the bottle reflects its power: sleek, heavy, and designed to look as refined as it smells.

Inspired by a garden after the rain, this new take on freshness leans heavy on the green and skips the citrus, which can overpower its subtle vibe. A hint of juicy pear adds light sweetness and a cooling effect that amplifies it. It also features a note called physcool, which is a chill, minty accord that reacts with the moisture on your skin to create a zingy tingle that drives home the fresh vibe. The result is a modern, versatile scent that works anywhere and on every guy.

I’ve never passed the folks playing chess in Washington Square Park and thought, “Man, I’d love to smell like those dudes.” But the strategy and tension of the game somehow inspired one of my favorite emerging fragrance houses, Mind Games. Its best release to date, Opera Mate, swaps checkmates for curtain calls, channeling the drama of the Paris Opera House into scent form. To me, it smells like a grand finale—elegant, layered, and impossible to ignore.

Opera Mate pulls me in from the first spray with creamy sandalwood and a touch of caramel that melt together into smooth, golden warmth. As it opens, roasted chestnut and grapefruit give it a lift, like a spark before the curtain rises. Then it deepens, revealing rich suede, smoky vetiver, and resinous benzoin that linger on the skin. It feels elegant yet bold, the kind of scent that commands attention without shouting. I wear it when I want to smell like confidence with a touch of drama.

This bottle is a loud, vibrant green reminiscent of Vulcan blood, which is fitting because it’s the logical choice for anyone looking for a refined, interesting scent. The scent itself is amber-woody, sure, but it’s a little spicy and bold without being obnoxious.

It opens with warm, resinous notes of Peru balsam, benzoin, and guaiac wood before evolving into green Bourbon geranium with rosy facets, while bergamot and musk add a fresh lift. It’s a collection of notes that feels like they shouldn’t work, but together create something powerful and new—one of those scents that’s hard to place in a single fragrance family.

When you think of aquatic scents, you typically think of notes like citrus, driftwood, and salty notes that mimic seawater. This surprising cologne, however, flips that idea on its head. Inspired by the Adriatic islands, there are notes of olive oil, fig, pine needles, cypress, and wild herbs. You still have a wet, oceanic quality that gives it an aquatic nature, but without citrus, the effect is earthier and more grounded, not to mention long-lasting and way more sophisticated. If you love fresh colognes but want to elevate your game, this one is for you.

Look, I get why the OG Bleu de Chanel is a classic fragrance; its blend of grapefruit, cedar, and sandalwood hits that sweet spot of being masculine without feeling like it’s begging for attention. But over the past couple of years since Bleu de Chanel L'Exclusif was released—and named a 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award winner—I found myself wearing it far more often.

It’s darker and denser, with much more staying power. The original Bleu de Chanel felt like a crisp summer morning, bright and fresh, whereas L'Exclusif is more like a windy, layered fall evening. It maintains some of the citrusy freshness of the original before evolving into something deeper, with sandalwood, leathery cistus labdanum, and woody amber notes taking over. It’s intense, aromatic, and guaranteed to make a statement.

While I love eating vanilla-flavored things (mostly ice cream, if I’m being honest), I was never a huge fan of the scent. This 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Award-winning cologne changed that for me—it’s easily the best vanilla fragrance I’ve worn. Don’t let the name fool you; the vanilla here isn’t the strongest note.

This cologne has a deep, leathery suede base layered with rich labdanum and amber notes for a masculine, cozy scent that’s perfect for cooler weather. The vanilla is just enough to spice things up from my usual leathery or amber colognes, but it doesn’t overpower the core of the fragrance. It’s strong too. A couple of sprays on my neck in the morning lasts me ten hours. Best part? It’s only $82. For a cologne of this quality, you usually have to spend at least twice that.

Read More: 2026 Men’s Health Grooming Awards

I’ve always loved the smell of campfire smoke; the deep, woody burn that clings to your clothes and stays in your memory. City on Fire captures this feeling better than any cologne I’ve ever tried, and I wear it year-round—bold in winter, magnetic in summer. It opens with spicy black pepper and dark berries before revealing layers of cardamom, labdanum, and clearwood that flicker like embers. The scent of cade oil and burnt match adds a rugged, smoldering edge that feels both primal and sophisticated.

Like all Imaginary Authors fragrances, it’s built around a story—in this case, a noir-like tale about two matchmakers drawn together by murder and mystery—and that narrative energy inspires the scent’s smoky, cinematic depth. I love how it lingers for hours, shifting from bright heat to soft ash, like the last glow of a fire you never want to leave. To be clear, this stuff is strong. If you’re not a fan of smoky fragrances, you’ll want to look elsewhere. But if you do dig a smoky cologne, this will quickly become a favorite.

Fragrance families are your roadmap to finding the right cologne. Once you figure out which group you’re drawn to, narrowing your search gets a whole lot easier. The four main families—fresh, floral, woody, and amber—cover almost every scent on the market, though some blends straddle more than one. You might also see fougère listed as a fifth family, but we treat it as a note within the woody category. Here’s how the big four break down:

Be it of the top, heart, or base variety, scent notes are far more specific than fragrance families, often referring to individual scent ingredients or aromas that make up a fragrance. The foundational notes of men’s cologne rarely change, but fragrance chemists (real thing!) are always updating the classics to build younger scents (also a thing!) that smell more modern. Of course, there are many more, but some key notes you’ll find in our favorite colognes are:

The eternal question when faced with purchasing any self-care product is what size to buy. When it comes to cologne, there are a few factors to keep in mind that’ll determine how big or small you’ll want to go here. For one, how often do you plan to wear the cologne? If you plan to make this your new daily scent, buy a bigger bottle so it’ll last longer.

But if you’re merely testing a fragrance or looking for something seasonal, consider a smaller option. Not to mention, cologne can run a bit expensive, especially for some of the stronger versions. So remember that buying a larger container can often offset some of the cost.

Cologne is personal, and what smells incredible on one guy might be missed entirely on another. That’s why the Men’s Health grooming team has been testing and debating scents nonstop since this story first ran in 2020. Over the years, we’ve sprayed, worn, and ranked hundreds of colognes across every fragrance family, taking notes on how they apply, evolve, and hold up through the day.

For this updated guide, I revisited our past favorites, compared them with new releases, and leaned on expert feedback to narrow it all down. Below, you’ll find the ten best colognes for men that are timeless, modern, and made to work in every season.

Apply cologne to the places where you can feel the beats of your heart. This means wrists, the sides of your neck, and over your ticker. The throb adds impact to the scent.

No cologne is perfect for every person, but there are a few best practices to follow when testing a new scent to find the right fit for you. For starters, don't bombard your skin with too many scents. When testing colognes, stick to no more than three on your skin so you can clearly tell each scent apart, says fragrance developer Ann Gottlieb.

So be selective with which you want to trial when browsing in-store because, as Gottlieb warns, testing too many too quickly can lead to nose fatigue. Gottlieb also recommends allowing a scent to linger on you for at least 30 minutes before deciding to buy. This lets you see how a fragrance reacts and develops with your own, unique body chemistry.
