#4776. How This Former Weightlifter Lost 80 Pounds After GLP-1s Stopped Working

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

For years, Dana Bichler was a competitive weightlifter. He felt fit and strong competing at 200 to 210 pounds. But wear and tear on his body and aging eventually pushed him to step away from weightlifting. Without the training, he began to gain weight slowly and steadily.

“I tried running, and a few other things, and the weight just crept up,” he told Healthline.

Dieting allowed him to lose about 50 pounds, but he would then regain it. At his heaviest, he weighed close to 300 pounds, which inspired him to visit a weight-loss clinic, where he followed a plan centered on the clinic’s foods.

“It’s a life of deprivation,” Bichler said. “You just can’t live like it.”

About five years ago, he tried a GLP-1 medication and two others a few years later. Each helped him lose weight initially but then stopped working.

“There was really no long-term positive effects or benefits that I saw,” he said.

However, he still takes Mounjaro for blood sugar control because he is prediabetic.

A few years ago, he was diagnosed with fatty liver disease. His condition was tied to obesity and caused scarring on his liver.

Bichler understood the seriousness of the condition as his two younger sisters and his oldest brother also had fatty liver disease. His brother and youngest sister developed cirrhosis, and his brother died after the disease affected other parts of his body.

“I had to do something,” he said. “What I was doing was not working.”

From his home in St. Cloud, Minnesota, Bichler traveled to the University of Minnesota to see a hepatologist, who referred him to a gastroenterologist who had worked with Boston Scientific on the instruments used to perform endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty (ESG).

ESG is a minimally invasive weight loss procedure performed using an FDA-authorized endoscopic suturing system, such as one offered through Boston Scientific’s Endura Weight Loss Solutions.

During ESG, a doctor passes an endoscope through the mouth and uses sutures to fold the stomach into a narrower sleeve. No portion of the stomach is removed, and there are no incisions. The smaller stomach limits how much a person can eat at once.

“Patients typically go home the same day and can return to routine daily activities within two to three days,” Brian Dunkin, MD, chief medical officer at Boston Scientific, told Healthline. “For the right person, that provides another less-invasive option to consider with their healthcare professional.”

While ESG may be a good option for some people who don’t achieve weight loss goals with GLP-1 medications, can’t tolerate them, or don’t want to stay on medication long term, Dunkin said he doesn’t think of it as ESG versus GLP-1 drugs.

“One of the best things GLP-1 medications have done is get more people talking to their doctors about obesity and recognizing it as a chronic disease that deserves treatment,” he said.

Each approach has different benefits, risks, and side effects.

“The goal is finding the right treatment, or combination of treatments, for the right patient at the right time,” said Dunkin.

ESG is indicated for adults with obesity with a BMI between 30 and 50, but Dunkin said BMI is only part of the conversation. ESG may be an option for people who aren’t getting the weight loss results they want, who don’t want to stay on weight loss medication long term, or for whom bariatric surgery may not be appropriate or desired, he added.

“Obesity is a chronic disease that requires long-term care,” said Dunkin. “ESG is one part of that care, which is why I believe so strongly in a multidisciplinary approach. The goal is to look at the whole person and find a care plan they can sustain over time.”

In March 2025, Bichler decided ESG was a good fit for him and received the procedure at Boston Scientific. At the time, he was 67 years old and on Medicare, which pre-approved the procedure.

“I just felt comfortable with it not being invasive, and I really needed to deal with [my weight], so I did,” he said.

When Bichler underwent ESG he weighed somewhere in the 260s. Today, he weighs 178 pounds.

While the procedure went smoothly, he said the following month was difficult. Because bread, pasta, rice, and carbonated drinks were off the table, he had to consume clear liquids, then slowly moved to other liquids, and eventually cream soups.

“I found that extremely difficult,” he said.

What surprised him most was depression. Looking back, he calls it a perfect storm. Working with his weight loss doctor, he had stopped taking his antidepressant about two weeks before the procedure. After surgery, his eating habits changed dramatically, disrupting the social life he’d built around food.

“I was in a pretty deep funk for a while,” he said. “I really was.”

He restarted his antidepressant, and over time, he adjusted to a new way of eating.

“I’ve discovered I like cream soup,” he said. “I still have it for meals.”

Although he’s lost more than 80 pounds, Bichler said the bigger change is how good he feels. He exercises four to five days a week and has more energy and moves more easily than he has in years.

“I haven’t felt this good in 30 years,” Bichler said. “I’m not kidding you.”

He’s able to enjoy things he loves like working on the farm he and his wife own. At the farm, he hunts ducks, turkeys, pheasants, and small game, and runs a trapline, all activities his weight had made nearly impossible for a long time.

“It used to be really hard for me to do because of the physicality of doing some of these things,” he said.

Although he retired from his profession, Bichler said he’s busier than ever. He’s a protodeacon in the Eastern Orthodox Church and also serves as a chaplain for his local police department, a role that has him climbing in and out of squad cars and up and down steps.

“Before I’d be sucking air trying to keep up,” he said.

Most meaningful of all is that he has more energy to give to his family.

“I have a grandson that I can actually do things and be active with now,” Bichler said. “It’s like starting all over. I just feel like a new person.”

#4775. DeepWay electric semi arrives in New Zealand, and gets a new name

New Zealand’s Foodstuffs North Island Limited has given its latest electric semi truck an electrifying new identity, courtesy of a second-grade student at a local elementary school.

The Chinese-built DeepWay Star began delivering chilled and frozen groceries across New Zealand’s lower North Island earlier this year – and, after a naming competition organized with students at Russell Street School in Palmerston North, the big HD EV has got a new name: Evie.

The winning name came from Year 2 (read: second grade) student named Madison, who beat out suggestions including Buzzy Bee, Lightning, and Bolt. Madison got to officially unveil the truck’s new name alongside her classmates, local officials and Foodstuffs representatives.

“Our trucks are out on the road every day delivering food to stores and communities, so we thought it would be great to get the kids involved and give our first electric truck a bit of personality,” explains Foodstuffs North Island General Manager Supply Chain, Yang Zhang. “There were some brilliant ideas, but Evie was a pretty fitting name for an EV. The best part is knowing Madison and the other students will be able to spot Evie out on the road and know they played a part in it.”

Madison was allowed to do the unveiling honors, revealing Evie’s new name alongside her other classmates, Palmerston North’s Mayor, Grant Smith, local MP Tangi Utikeri, and local PAK’nSAVE, New World, and Four Square grocers who will be receiving deliveries from Evie.

In its first few months on the road, Evie’s travelled nearly 45,000 kilometers (~28,000 miles) and avoided more than 81,000 kg of harmful carbon emissions – which the company claims is roughly equivalent to taking 35 ICE cars off the road for a full year.

As for the truck itself, it has a sort of Tesla-ish, anteater-y look, and significantly longer range than the StarWay, offering more than 500 km (~310 miles) of range from its 600 kWh CATL-built LFP battery packs that can plug into charge ports two at a time for lickety-quick charging in about 30 minutes. If that’s too long of a wait, the Star can swap its tired batteries for fresh ones in special battery-sway stations in just six minutes.

The DeepWay’s electric motors put out 491 kW (~660 hp) of power, and a positively tectonic 75,000 (!) Nm (~55,000 lb-ft) (!!) of torque – more than enough to get the 50 tons (100,000 lb.) of GVWR it’s rated for up to speed.

It is great to see electric trucks replacing Diesel. I just can’t understand why EV adoption is so slow to take off in New Zealand. It has plenty of great low cost EVs and petrol is all imported and expensive.

You can check out the pictures, above, then let us know what you think of the big Chinese BEV and it’s fun new name in the comments.

#4774. Electric cars are about to overtake petrol in the UK, data shows

Battery-electric cars took 32% of the UK’s new car market in October, while petrol cars fell to just 37.2%, according to new data from the SMMT. That’s the closest the two have been.

At the current pace, electric cars will outsell petrol in the UK within a year. And it could happen as soon as this December.

The UK registered 152,730 new cars in October, up 5.4% year-over-year and the 11th straight month of growth for the overall market.

All of that growth came from plug-ins. BEV registrations jumped 32.7% to 48,858 units, and plug-in hybrids rose 30.1% to 22,898. Meanwhile, petrol fell 11.6% to 56,876 units, diesel dropped 15.9%, and even conventional hybrids were down 5%.

Through the first 10 months of the year, the UK has now registered 503,805 BEVs, up 30.4%, for a 26.6% market share. Petrol’s year-to-date share is down to 41.1%, from 47.2% at the same point last year.

We pulled SMMT’s monthly fuel-type data going back to March 2024 to see where this is heading. Note that SMMT counts mild hybrids as petrol (or diesel) in its headline categories, and that’s generally how we count them at Electrek.

In March 2024, petrol held 55.9% of the market and BEVs 15.2%. In October 2026, it was 37.2% vs 32.0%. Petrol’s share is shrinking by about half a point per month on a linear trend, while BEVs gain about 0.36 points a month. Extend both lines and they cross around August 2027 at roughly 33% each.

But that’s the slow scenario, because it ignores December.

UK BEV share spikes every December as automakers push volume to get closer to their ZEV Mandate targets. BEVs hit 31.0% in December 2024 and 32.2% in December 2025, when petrol was at 39.4%. Over the last five months, BEV share has run about 5 points higher than a year earlier, and petrol about 7 points lower. If December follows that pattern, BEVs land around 37% and petrol around 32%.

That would be the first time BEVs beat petrol in SMMT’s headline numbers, mild hybrids included.

However, SMMT’s own forecast of 27.2% BEV share for the full year implies roughly 31% for November and December combined, which would make it a much closer call. And on a stricter definition that puts mild hybrids with hybrids instead of petrol, BEVs already outsold every other powertrain in August.

Zoom out to full years and the picture is just as clear. Cars that run only on petrol or diesel, mild hybrids included, made up 72.5% of the UK market in 2021. This year, they’re at 45.5%.

None of this is good enough for the SMMT, which is using the release to push the government, again, to cut the ZEV Mandate targets.

The mandate requires 33% of 2026 sales to be zero-emission. SMMT now forecasts 27.2%. It expects 32% next year against a 38% target, and 37.5% in 2028 against 52%, a 14.5-point gap.

The trade group says automakers have spent “billions” on discounts, 0% financing, deposit contributions, and even subsidized charging to move EVs, on top of the government’s Electric Car Grant. It also slammed last week’s Budget, which confirmed a new EV-specific road tax (eVED) starting in 2028 and kept 20% VAT on public charging.

“Higher targets may force supply, but they do not create demand,” SMMT chief executive Mike Hawes said.

We’ve heard this one before. The SMMT made the same argument after September’s record 99,199 BEV registrations, and the government already opened a review of the mandate this year.

This might be the main reason why the trade group wants to slow things down. The brands growing fastest in the UK are mostly Chinese. BYD registered 6,065 cars in October, up 73%. Jaecoo more than doubled to 6,089 units, Chery nearly tripled to 3,707, and Leapmotor doubled to 1,773. MG was up 85%.

Tesla, on the other hand, registered just 282 cars in October, down 45% from 511 a year ago. The first month of the quarter is always slow for Tesla in the UK, and the brand is still up 31% year-to-date at 46,526 units after a big September. But it didn’t have a single model in October’s top 10 BEVs, which was led by the Skoda Enyaq (1,568), Mini Countryman (1,494), and Jaecoo 5 (1,465).

The SMMT’s framing is that there’s a “demand gap.” The data shows the opposite. BEV registrations are up 30% this year while petrol is shrinking every single month. That’s not a market rejecting EVs.

The SMMT is not a neutral organisation, they have been briefing against EVs for years and continue to do so.

The ZEV mandate is NOT a measure of how many pure BEVs are sold, and the SMMT know it, it's a measure of REDUCING emission against a level set in the past.

Those emissions reductions can be met by selling BEVs, or selling more efficient PHEVs or even selling more efficient petrol or diesel cars! The manufacturers can also buy credits if they choose to.

NO manufacturer has paid any ZEV fines to date (DfT announcement March 2026)

As for the "heavy discounts" and "loss making sales", well I have two data points on that.

1. The retail price of EVs has continued to climb in the UK over the past 6 years, despite the cost of any average 50kWh battery pack dropping several thousand dollars.

2. There are hundreds of main dealerships who are buying cars from the manufacturers, driving them for the minimum 3 month period, often with just a few thousand miles on the clock and then selling them with a 30-35% retail price discount, and then repeating ad infinitum. The dealerships are still making a few thousand with each transaction, so we know where the manufacturers price really sits.

And the discounts automakers keep complaining about? That’s the mandate doing exactly what it was designed to do. It forces automakers to sell EVs, so they price them to sell, and buyers respond. Hawes says targets don’t create demand, but cheaper EVs clearly do. October proves it.

Now, is the jump to 52% in 2028 steep? It is steep, but it looks achievable to me. If anything is hurting demand, it’s the government’s own moves: a new EV-only road tax and 20% VAT on public charging. That’s what the industry should be fighting. It’s too early for that.

Either way, petrol’s days as the UK’s default car are numbered. The only question is whether the milestone comes in December or sometime in 2027. Our bet is December.

This multi-purpose option contains all the ingredients you want in an eye cream, like niacinamide, hyaluronic acid, and ceramides, to help reduce puffiness and dark circles and keep the skin around your eyes hydrated and happy for under $15. In short, it solves a bunch of different skin issues at a price point that's hard to beat.

The well-rounded ingredients address all sorts of issues from dark circles to eye bags and everything in between. Keep in mind that it likely won’t give you instantaneous results thanks to the gentler formula (and lower price point), but with consistent use, it can improve the overall look of your eye area. Another thing to keep in mind: this is thick, possibly even too thick to use during the day if you have oily skin or just don’t like the feel of heavy creams on your face.

Read More: How to Build Skincare Routine Under $50

The Atwater Eye Moisturizer is a compact, travel-ready solution for tired eyes brought on by a long flight or drive. Formulated with peptides, amino acids, and antioxidants, it helps firm, lift, and smooth fine lines and wrinkles for a refreshed look. There’s also caffeine that works to reduce puffiness and dark circles by tightening the skin and improving circulation.

The 0.5 oz tube is ideal for travel, easily fitting into any Dopp kit or toiletry bag. Plus, its sturdy cap feels leak-proof, ensuring it stays secure on the go. Also, the formula is non-comedogenic (so it won’t clog pores), hypoallergenic, and fragrance-free, so it’s gentle on sensitive skin. It’s my go-to eye cream whenever I’m traveling.

Dwayne ‘The Rock’ Johnson is known for many things: natural charisma, action movies seemingly predestined to make bank, and biceps the size of basketballs. But he’s been in the public eye for so long, it often goes unremarked that his now 53-year-old face looks nearly identical to what it was in the late nineties. So, after years of being asked about his skincare routine, he decided to drop his own brand last year with Papatui. And no product represents his age-defying attributes more than its unscented eye cream.

Dispensed through a slick, easy-to-use metal roller, the gel-like cream glides effortlessly around the eyes with an immediate awakening sensation. For this, you can thank its combination of skin-hydrating hyaluronic acid, protective ectoin (an amino acid that helps reinforce the skin’s natural barrier), and alerting caffeine. Best of all, it’s completely unscented, so those with sensitive skin will see no reaction or irritation.

A lot of unscented eye creams still have a slight chemical smell to them, but this option is truly scentless. Also, unlike many others, you don’t seem to have to pay a few more bucks for the lack of fragrance. It’s an incredible value at $10, especially considering that I can get weeks out of one container while using it every day.

When it comes to luxury skincare brands for men, few are more reliable than Patricks. Whether it’s an ultra-foamy body wash with a cologne-quality scent or hair-thickening shampoo that actually does plump up strands, the brand always ensures its quality matches its price point. So whenever Patricks launches a new product, I pay attention. Its latest release? ES2 Ultra-Smoothing Eye Serum, and it did not disappoint.

Now back and better than ever, the ES2 delivers seamless execution and even better visible results. The non-greasy formula, led by hero ingredients glycerin and niacinamide, works to combat any issue you’re facing by reducing puffiness, fighting dark circles, and minimizing wrinkles. The application is effortless thanks to a sleek, metal rollerball applicator that cools and depuffs the under-eye area while delivering just the right amount of serum.

After consistent use for a month, I noticed a clear improvement: reduced puffiness, smoother texture, and a brighter, more youthful appearance under the eyes. It’s an effective, no-fuss solution for anyone looking to tackle fine lines and revitalize tired-looking eyes.

There’s certainly no shortage of eye creams out there, but when you’re choosing the right eye cream for you, the biggest things to consider are why and when you’re going to use it.

Depending on what you’re hoping to address with an eye cream, you’ll want to look for certain ingredients.

The ingredients in the formula will inform you when it is best to use that specific eye cream. For instance, retinol should only be used at night because it can make skin more sensitive to sunlight. Other ingredients, like SPF, are unnecessary to use at night. Most eye creams, however, can be used both day and night, so the other factor you might want to consider is weight. Wearing a heavy eye cream during the day may feel uncomfortable, whereas a lighter, gel formula might not be hydrating enough for night use.

Compared to daily moisturizers, eye creams can often cost more, largely because they're formulated to target signs of aging around the delicate eye area. That said, they can be well worth the investment. To get the most value, pay attention to the product size. While larger tubes may seem pricey upfront, they usually last longer, saving you money over time. On the other hand, if you travel frequently or have limited counter space, a smaller container will be the better choice.

As a dude in his thirties, crow’s feet and I have officially started our long-term relationship. We’ve moved on from casual coffee dates after long nights of drinking in my twenties to more serious, regular meals. As such, I’ve been trying eye creams for years now.

For this story specifically, I also consulted with fellow Men’s Health writers on what products they prefer. Based on this intel, along with some of my go-tos, I evaluated over 50 eye creams on how they felt when applied, their ingredients, and how effective they were at reducing wrinkles, fine lines, and dark circles. After a year of this research and testing, I’ve chosen the following nine as the best night creams for men to buy in 2026.

Generally, you want to be very gentle when applying eye cream because the skin around your eyes is thinner and more delicate than the skin on the rest of your face. Pulling and tugging can increase issues like sagging or wrinkles over time. The best way to apply eye cream is by using your ring finger and using a gentle tapping motion. Use a pea-sized amount (you don’t need more than that, as eye creams tend to be very concentrated) and gently tap it onto your skin with your ring finger, starting at the inner corner of your eye and working outward. Follow under your eye, then work up to the corner and finally up to just under your brow bone (think of it as a big circle around your eye).One caveat here: if your eye cream is a tube with an applicator tip (bonus points if it’s a cooling metal tip or rollerball), you don’t need to use your fingers. Smooth it directly onto your skin using the applicator, but remember to apply minimal pressure. If you need to rub it in a bit more, use a tapping motion.

There’s no perfect age to start using an eye cream, but it’s always easier to prevent than to treat signs of skin aging. For this reason, starting an eye cream in the 20s-30s can be helpful, says dermatologist Dr. Marisa Garshick, MD. That said, it’s also never too late to start, so if you’re just starting to notice crow’s feet or dark circles, it is fine to start at any age.

I get the appeal of using moisturizer as an eye cream to save time and money. However, dermatologist Dr. Bradley Glodny recommends a separate product designed specifically for the delicate under-eye area. Eye creams are formulated with targeted ingredients to address common concerns like puffiness, dark circles, and fine lines. And because this skin is especially sensitive, regular facial moisturizers can often be too harsh. For most men, a dedicated under-eye cream is the better choice.

#4772. The Psychology of Miracles

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

The human psyche has always upheld a tireless faith in the extraordinary. When tragic events decimate our sense of safety and security, such as an unexpected medical diagnosis, a devastating personal crisis, or a profound loss, we seldom default to reason. Instead, we survey horizons looking for signs and wishing for the seemingly impossible to step in and rescue us from the inevitable.

This reaction is not rare. Surveys from Gallup and Pew Research show that up to 79 percent of U.S. adults believe in miracles, while more than 67 percent strongly believe in phenomena beyond scientific explanation. When reason falls arguably short, divine intervention becomes the next best thing.

For millennia, our existence has relied heavily on our ancestors’ ability to anticipate threats and secure their surroundings. This important skill helped to avoid near-certain death from starvation or the elements, in the event we were ostracized from our tribe. The robust urge to create some kind of order in a confusing and hostile world was paramount. Consequently, strict cause-and-effect accounts often fall emotionally flat. Whenever we are confronted with catastrophic hardship or existential dread, statistics might explain how an event occurred, but oftentimes it can't answer more profound human questions.

Whenever human beings reframe a striking coincidence as divine intervention or maybe even the hand of God, you have to wonder: Is it simply impulsive denial, or is it a hardwired inclination to believe in the supernatural? Accordingly, it's hard to negate the obvious that perhaps miracles act as psychological defense mechanisms—safeguards explicitly designed to protect us from crippling despair. That's why we so often hear overused proverbs like “Everything happens for a reason” and “God works in mysterious ways.”

Whenever we utilize this defense mechanism, the human mind reclaims a sense of agency when circumstances beyond our control leave us feeling powerless. Anticipating miracles helps to regulate the body's built-in stress response by lowering cortisol levels (the stress hormone) and sustaining emotional stamina during prolonged crisis. It's part of our evolutionary adaptation—a sophisticated cognitive mechanism intended to stimulate hope, develop resilience, and drive us forward even when the odds are stacked against us. Novelist and philosopher Fyodor Dostoevsky, who profoundly examined human psychology, wrote, “since man cannot live without miracles, he will provide himself with miracles of his own making."

But like most things in life, there are downsides to having a miracle mindset. Shielding us from hopelessness and relying too heavily on the mystical can pose psychological, medical, and existential risks. For instance, individuals might reject evidence-based medical treatments, therapeutic interventions, and, perhaps, lifesaving procedures by instead waiting for an unlikely intervention from above.

Additionally, it can lead to passivity and hesitation when needing to assert free will in making important decisions. It could also cause spiritual injury because when anticipated miracles fail to happen, the ensuing fallout can be debilitating. In place of organically processing grief, people might also assume cosmic guilt, blaming themselves or believing their faith was not strong enough. This could potentially worsen their trauma.

The miracle mindset could also foster detachment from reality, ignoring hard facts, leaving individuals vulnerable to exploitation by predatory people, control groups, and buying into false promises. In the end, it could train the mind to overlook sound rationality and established scientific data that is invaluable to our health and well-being.

In America, presenting cold, hard facts to people who are deeply entrenched in their beliefs can trigger a reaction. For many, perhaps it feels too much like an existential threat, frequently promoting defensiveness and condemnation. Whenever we challenge any kind of sacred doctrine, we invite accusations of blasphemy or a lack of a moral compass.

Our personal beliefs are much more than just opinions. They are vital pillars of safety, identity, and communal belonging. Science demonstrates that when an overpoweringly held worldview is questioned, the brain processes it like a threat of physical danger. It does not compute it as a rational debate, but as a menace to psychological existence.

Finally, believing in miracles fulfills a human need that offers structure and comfort. It helps us manage the fear of what lies beyond more easily. The idea of a meaningless, dark oblivion that lacks determination is hard for many people to swallow. Hence, the concept of divine intervention acts as a soothing balm against uncertainty, providing reassurance in a shaky and unpredictable world.

In addition, every human being feels the omnipresent specter of death. The anxiety around mortality will always be something we have in common. But what separates us is the degree to which we allow fear to govern our choices and our worldviews and how it might compromise our ability to exercise our own free will.

Therefore, how we respond to it is wholly a choice. Perhaps the true measure of our freedom is not how we escape our fear of mortality, but how we live it every day, in spite of it. And sometimes, enduring that reality requires a trace of the supernatural. There’s no harm in a spark of magic in the midst of inescapable tragedy.

As the saying goes (often credited to Albert Einstein), "There are only two ways to live your life: One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle.”

#4771. Toyota updates the 2027 RAV4 PHEV with an NACS port and up to 52 miles of EV range

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 is bringing a few major updates, including an added NACS charge port on all plug-in hybrid (PHEV) models.

The RAV4 was Toyota’s best-selling nameplate in the US last year and consistently ranks among America’s most popular vehicles alongside the Ford F-Series and Chevrolet Silverado.

For the 2027 model year, Toyota added several notable upgrades. The 2027 Toyota RAV4 will be available with hybrid (HEV) and plug-in hybrid (PHEV) powertrains, with available front- or all-wheel drive (AWD).

The biggest change is that all 2027 RAV4 PHEV models now have a built-in NACS charge port with Level 3 DC fast-charging capabilities.

The NACS port is on the driver’s side and lets drivers use Tesla Superchargers without a separate adapter. All PHEV grades also include an 11 kW onboard AC charger.

Powered by Toyota’s sixth-generation PHEV system, the plug-in RAV4 has standard AWD with a combined output of 321 horsepower. The setup includes a 2.5-liter four-cylinder engine, two electric motors, and a high-capacity traction battery.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 PHEV offers up to 52 miles of pure electric range on the base SE trim. It will be available in four trims: SE, XSE, Woodland, and GR Sport.

Toyota updated the suspension system in the Woodland grade for the 2027 model year with new springs, shocks, and jounce bumpers, giving it 9.1″ of ground clearance.

The Woodland trim adds a rugged look with standard All-Terrain tires, Roof Rails with Cross Bars, and a Tow Hitch Receiver. It also features new all-weather floor and cargo mats.

Lastly, the RAV4 GR Sport trim is for those who want a more performance-oriented, sporty style, with GT-tuned suspension and steering, sports seating, and a standard PHEV powertrain with AWD.

Inside, the 2027 RAV4 includes a standard 12.3″ digital cluster and a 10.5″ touchscreen with the Toyota Audio Multimedia system, plus wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto.

A 12.9″ touchscreen with a JBL Premium Audio system with 9 speakers is standard on the Limited trim and available on the XSE grade.

All 2027 Toyota RAV4s come with standard Toyota Safety Sense 4.0, which includes safety and convenience features such as Lane Departure Alert with Steering Assist, Full-Speed Range Dynamic Radar Cruise Control, Proactive Driving Assist, and a Pre-Collision System with Pedestrian Detection.

They don't make it easy to find out just what that level 3 charging rate is or how big the battery is. If it's as slow as an old Bolt, could take as long as 20 minutes to charge. If the DC charge hardware is more modern, could be 5-10. Would still be a weird choice, but if you need to stop for a drink of a bathroom anyway, why not?

2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV models are expected to begin arriving at dealerships later this year, while the PHEV models are expected to follow in early 2027.

The 2027 Toyota RAV4 HEV starts at $32,300 (LE FWD), and the PHEV version starts at $42,100, not including the $1,595 destination fee.

#4770. Hormone Therapy May Boost Weight Loss on Wegovy, But Not as Much on Zepbound

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Females using menopause hormone therapy (MHT) alongside GLP-1 medications such as Ozempic or Wegovy may experience greater weight loss, according to a study presented at the 2026 Annual Meeting of the Menopause Society.

Weight gain is a common concern among middle-aged women. While much of this is associated with aging, hormonal changes during menopause can also contribute to changes in body fat and its distribution.

GLP-1 medications have been shown to be effective for weight loss. However, the results may vary by sex and reproductive stage.

For example, studies have found that women and adults under age 55 may experience greater weight loss with these medications.

A previous small observational study in postmenopausal women found that using MHT alongside semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, was associated with greater weight loss.

However, whether hormone therapy influences weight loss outcomes with different GLP-1 medications remains unclear.

To investigate this question, researchers compared weight loss in middle-aged women receiving either semaglutide or tirzepatide, with or without MHT. The findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.

The study included 3,855 women with an average age of 57 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 36 kg/m2.

The semaglutide cohort included 2,379 individuals, while the tirzepatide cohort included 1,476 individuals.

The average follow-up in the semaglutide cohort, both with and without MHT, was 26 months. The average follow-up in the tirzepatide group was 17 months for those using MHT and 16 months for those not using it.

The researchers found that in the semaglutide cohort, those using MHT alongside the GLP-1 medication had significantly greater weight loss at 9 months than those not using MHT.

These differences were sustained at 12 and 15 months and at the final follow-up. Those using MHT were also more likely to reach up to a 30% total body weight loss than those not using it.

In the tirzepatide cohort, those using MHT had a modestly greater weight loss at 3 months and were more likely to achieve more than 5% total body weight loss by the final follow-up. However, no significant difference in weight loss was observed at later time points.

These findings suggest that MHT use may be associated with greater weight loss among middle-aged women taking semaglutide. However, the researchers did not observe a sustained, statistically significant difference in weight loss among those taking tirzepatide.

Betul Hatipoglu, MD, Director of the Diabetes and Obesity Center at the University Hospitals Cleveland Medical Center, who was not involved in the study, told Healthline that the findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that people should be careful not to interpret them as evidence that hormone therapy should be added to GLP-1 treatment specifically to enhance weight loss.

“This is an association, and the study provides an opportunity to discuss how menopause, aging, changes in body composition, and metabolic health can be present,” she said.

It is important to keep in mind that the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved certain hormone therapy medications to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes, night sweats, and vaginal dryness. However, these medications are not FDA-approved for weight loss or obesity management.

The study authors noted that larger studies are needed to confirm their observations and to inform individualized strategies for middle-aged females.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB-GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who was not involved in the study, noted that weight gain is one of the most common concerns she hears from women during menopause. Beyond affecting self-esteem and quality of life, excess abdominal fat can increase the risk of type 2 diabetes and heart disease.

“Finding effective, sustainable ways to manage weight is important for women’s long-term health and healthy aging,” she said.

“I would like to see prospective, randomized studies examining GLP-1 medications with and without hormone therapy to determine whether hormone therapy directly improves weight loss and helps women maintain it over time. In the meantime, treatment decisions should be individualized and guided by a healthcare professional.”

Ross advised that the decision should be based on your individual symptoms, health history, and treatment goals.

“Hormone therapy can significantly improve disruptive menopausal symptoms, including hot flashes, sleep disturbances, and mood changes. By helping women feel better and more energetic, it may also make it easier to exercise and manage their weight,” she said.

Hatipoglu noted that GLP-1-based medications, on the other hand, are effective treatments for obesity and can improve important aspects of metabolic health. Their use should be based on an individual’s weight-related health risks, medical history, and treatment goals.

“For a woman who has both bothersome menopausal symptoms and obesity, it may be entirely appropriate to consider both treatments. But I would not recommend starting hormone therapy solely to improve the weight-loss response to a GLP-1 medication based on the evidence currently available,” she said.

“It is also important to remember that successful weight management during and after menopause is about more than the number on the scale. Preserving muscle mass, maintaining bone health, improving metabolic health, and supporting long-term physical function are equally important.”

You should speak with your healthcare professional about the risks and benefits of all treatment options.

#4769. Robert Pattinson Is Officially the Next James Bond. Director James Gray Believes He Can Pull It Off.

“What Rob does have is something enigmatic about him,” Pattinson’s Lost City of Z director says. “And that enigmatic quality, I think, might serve very well for that.”

THE LONG SEARCH for a new James Bond has finally come to an end: Robert Pattinson will play the world’s most famous spy in the new installment from director Denis Villeneuve. His casting marks the conclusion of a race that not too long ago looked to be down to a trio of contenders—Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor—to go along with a “mystery candidate.” Now, the man of mystery can claim victory (Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were both revealed as late-in-the-game candidates to play 007).

Pattinson, who first achieved fame as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire in 2005 before skyrocketing to another level with the Twilight franchise starting in 2008, has spent the last 15 years establishing himself as perhaps our most unique and eccentric actor, a uniquely handsome talent who seems to relish in playing a series of freaks, weirdos, and deviants. Roles in movies like Josh and Benny Safdie’s Good Time and Robert Eggers’s The Lighthouse made it abundantly clear that Pattinson’s talent and ambition reach far beyond the franchises for which he initially gained recognition.

One of Pattinson’s best roles in that period came in 2016’s The Lost City of Z, an adventure film (based on the nonfiction book of the same name) from director James Gray. In Lost City, Pattinson plays Henry Costin, the eccentric assistant to Charlie Hunnam’s lead explorer Percy Fawcett.

In making Lost City of Z, Gray got an up-close opportunity to work with Pattinson and see just what he’s capable of as an actor. “The character he was playing with me—this bearded, oddball, left field explorer type—is so different from Bond,” Gray tells Men’s Health. “But that doesn’t mean he couldn’t do it. What Rob does have is something enigmatic about him. And that enigmatic quality, I think, might serve very well for that.”

Gray, who spoke with MH just a few days ahead of Pattinson’s official casting when speculation was at its peak, was fully confident in the 40-year-old’s ability to pull just about any role off, calling him a “fabulous actor,” and reflecting fondly on their time working together in the jungle.

“Look, they will know,” Gray continues. “I mean, Denis [Villeneuve] will know, he’s probably screen-tested already. I haven’t talked to him about it, but I’m sure he’s looked at all these screen tests, and it’s a thing that you know immediately when you see it on the big screen.”

Gray was onto something, as Pattinson has now officially been cast as the seventh actor to play James Bond, following in the footsteps of only Sean Connery, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton, Pierce Brosnan, and Daniel Craig.

Pattinson is at the tail end of what’s been a truly remarkable year, starring in The Drama, The Odyssey, and Primetime, with a villainous supporting role in Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three still to come.

It’s also worth noting that Pattinson’s output hasn’t exclusively been weirdos and oddballs (although it is also worth noting that at one point he had a streak where his characters kept masturbating on screen in every movie). The Batman he proved he can expertly lead one of pop culture’s biggest and most valuable franchises in a way that he made totally his own (and is currently in the process of filming that film’s long-in-the-making sequel), and his role as Neil in Christopher Nolan’s Tenet may as well have been his unofficial Bond audition. Pattinson’s sleek, funny, and cool as hell as a time-traveling secret agent in that film, looking handsome and dapper along the way.

Gray himself is no stranger to talented actors; his latest film, Paper Tiger, pairs Adam Driver and Miles Teller. But he emphasizes the mere fact that Villeneuve and the film’s producers had Pattinson screen test for the role. “It means that they saw something special in him,” he says. “I’m sure he could pull it off—he’s a brilliant actor.”

#4768. New Jersey is putting 10 MW of community solar on warehouse roofs

Warehouse roofs are prime real estate for solar, and Faropoint is putting more of that underused space to work in New Jersey. The industrial property owner has started construction on the first of 16 community solar projects totaling more than 10 megawatts (MW).

First up is a 1.6 MW rooftop array at 19-05 Nevins Road in Fair Lawn. Another 15 projects, totaling about 8.5 MW, have been accepted into New Jersey’s Community Solar Energy Program, and nine are already cleared to start construction.

That’s more solar going onto buildings that are already there, with participating households set to get savings on their electricity bills.

Large warehouse roofs offer something solar developers need: lots of flat space. Putting panels up there gives the same building the job of generating electricity without taking up additional land.

Faropoint specializes in industrial properties used for local deliveries and distribution. “Utilizing previously unused portions of our buildings allows us to support the communities where we invest,” said Brian Nave, Faropoint’s vice president of asset management and renewable energy.

Faropoint and its independent solar adviser, SolarKal, expect the 16 projects to generate around 12.7 million kilowatt-hours (kWh) of electricity annually once they’re operating. They estimate the portfolio will avoid about 8,500 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions a year.

Faropoint says at least half of each project’s capacity will be reserved for low- and moderate-income households. New Jersey’s program requires a minimum of 51%.

#4767. Why the Clever Hans Analogy Fails Nonspeaking Spellers

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 16, 2026 | Reviewed by Abigail Fagan

Every time nonspeaking people with autism who spell to communicate make the news, someone brings up Clever Hans. You may know the story: In early 1900s Berlin, a horse seemed to do math, tapping out answers with his hoof. In 1907, the psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed what was really going on. When the questioner knew the answer and Hans could see them, Hans was right about 89% of the time; when the questioner didn't know, or Hans wore blinders, he dropped to about 6%. Questioners unknowingly leaned forward while he tapped and relaxed when he reached the right number, and Hans had learned to stop there.

The suggestion is that spellers are doing the same thing: that the words really come from the person holding the letterboard, either through subtle cues or through the communication partner's unconscious movements (the ideomotor effect). In this post, I draw on my own data and on a year of observations of nonspeaking autistic people to show why this analogy doesn't hold, and why it should be dropped for good. This is not only my personal opinion that comparing nonspeaking autistic people to a horse is cruel; it is also what the facts show.

Hans's trick worked because his task was simple: all he needed was a signal telling him when to stop tapping. Spelling is a different kind of task. To spell a sentence, a person has to choose the right letter out of 26, in the right order, again and again. A single "stop" cue, the kind that worked for Hans, can't do that. Add to this complex dance the sentences that contain words the communication partner doesn't know or normally use, or information nobody in the room expected to hear.

The best evidence here comes from studies that measured how spellers actually spell. In 2020, Vikram Jaswal and his colleagues fitted nine nonspeaking autistic letterboard users with head-mounted eye-trackers while they answered questions about an article read aloud to them, with an assistant holding the board.¹ They pointed to about one letter per second, and 94% of the letters they pointed to were correct. On average, they looked at 71% of the correct letters before pointing to them, about half a second ahead. Like fluent non-autistic typists, they paused longer before the first letter of a new word and were faster on common letter pairs. As the authors point out, cueing would require a separate signal for every letter, picked from 26 options, which would be slow and error-prone. What they found was fast, accurate, and planned.

Some critics argue that the partner moves the board slightly toward the right letter. A 2024 study from the same lab removed the partner entirely.² Thirty-one nonspeaking autistic teenagers and adults played a game on an iPad mounted on a stand, tapping letters as they lit up. No one held the iPad. As a group, they tapped faster when the letters spelled a sentence they had just heard than when similar letters or symbols came in a meaningless order. They were also faster on common letter pairs, and they paused before the first letter of each new word. These are signs of knowing how to spell.

A third study had participants spell on a virtual letterboard in an augmented-reality headset, with no one holding it; they averaged 95.8% accuracy on dictated words.³

If spellers were reading their partners the way Hans read his questioners, blocking their view of the partner should stop them, just as the blinders stopped Hans. As it happens, we've been testing this with a few spellers by placing a rigid panel, about five feet tall and three feet wide, between the speller and the communication partner, so that the spellers cannot see the partners' faces or bodies. The results? They keep spelling fluently and without hesitation. After the very first word, one of them even spelled: "Better with the barrier."

The second problem with the horse analogy is the content. Hans only ever answered questions, and only with answers the questioner already had in mind. Spellers start conversations, ask for things, and say things that surprise the people around them.

A young man I visited this year began spelling at fifteen and spells mainly with his mother. After I spent a full day visiting him at school, he was able that evening to have a conversation about his day and to spell the names of two kids who had visited the classroom; neither his mother nor I knew their names, and his mother hadn't been at school. He was also able to express his feelings towards his brothers and his wish for more independence: "I'm seventeen, let me go by myself," he spelled when he asked to walk to the bus stop alone. Among his other wishes, he asked to go into the ocean with his brothers, wearing a life jacket, and told his parents he wanted a North Face backpack, not the Under Armour one they had picked.

When his mother first began spelling with him on her own, one of his first requests was to see a Broadway show, which she had never imagined he wanted. He also spelled things his partner would not choose to hear. In front of me, he told his mother that a book I'd brought was boring, and she was embarrassed. On another occasion, when he came downstairs while his mother was out, he spelled to his father: "Dad, stop giving me chicken nuggets. I just want to spend time together."

But perhaps his most unexpected request came when he spelled out that he wanted to go to Disney World for his sixteenth birthday, something the family would never have expected, given his sensitivity to crowded and noisy places. They went; he wore noise-cancelling headphones, and he had a blast. "I tolerated it because I wanted to be there," he told me, and made fun of how his father threw up on rides.

A cueing account says the words come from his mother's expectations. However, these messages went against what his family expected, and they changed how the family lives with him. This is exactly what we should be looking for when we ask whether a speller is the author of their words: requests, opinions, and jokes that the partner did not anticipate and would not have chosen. The Hans model has no way to produce them.

Comparing a person to a horse responding to signals is not a neutral choice. It fits an old and outdated assumption: that people who don't speak don't understand. For decades, nonspeaking autistic people were labeled profoundly intellectually disabled, often without any assessment that accommodated their motor differences. The young man I visited spent his early school years in a program built around life skills and weather charts, and he calls his current high school classroom what it is: segregated. When a speller's words are dismissed with a one-line reference to Clever Hans, the speller pays the price: in which school they attend, whether their requests are taken seriously, and whether anyone asks for their opinion at all.

And, if you are still not convinced after reading this, perhaps hearing from the nonspeakers themselves will help. Here’s what they have been expressing about the effects of spelling on their lives:

"It was a game changer for me. It provided me with freedom I dreamed about for 15 years. Now, instead of being an observer, I am an active participant."

"Learning to spell changed my life trajectory. Before, I was treated like a toddler, and my world collapsed in on me… doctors, experts, teachers got it all wrong.… So communication is not just a basic need but a human right."

1. Jaswal, V. K., Wayne, A., & Golino, H. (2020). Eye-tracking reveals agency in assisted autistic communication. Scientific Reports, 10, 7882.

2. Jaswal, V. K., Lampi, A. J., & Stockwell, K. M. (2024). Literacy in nonspeaking autistic people. Autism, 28(10), 2503–2514.

3. Alabood, L., Dow, T., Feeley, K. B., Jaswal, V. K., & Krishnamurthy, D. (2024). From letterboards to holograms: Advancing assistive technology for nonspeaking autistic individuals with the HoloBoard. In Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '24). ACM. https://doi.org/10.1145/3613904.3642626

#4766. Segway launches new electric motorcycle that’s so safe it has seatbelts

Segway came to EICMA this year with a surprisingly broad lineup of new electric motorcycles, ranging from high-performance concepts to off-road machines. But perhaps the most interesting of the bunch is also the one that looks the least like a conventional motorcycle or scooter.

Meet the Segway X Cruiser, an electric two-wheeler that takes motorcycle safety so seriously that it has a roll cage and seatbelts.

Or at least, those are among the configurations Segway is showing as it develops the new machine for production.

The X Cruiser is Segway’s attempt to bring more automotive-style protection to a single-track vehicle, essentially asking how much of a car’s safety envelope can be wrapped around a motorcycle without adding another pair of wheels.

From the looks of things, the answer is quite a lot.

Segway says the X Cruiser’s design was informed by automotive crash scenarios, with cage and semi-cage structures, four-direction collision protection, staged energy absorption, and seatbelt restraints intended to improve rider protection. It also gets active safety features including standard blind spot detection and lane change warning.

The company showed several ways that basic idea can be configured, ranging from a more conventional partially enclosed scooter-like setup to versions with significantly more structure surrounding the rider. One of the most striking configurations uses a heavily bolstered race-car-style seat and seatbelt along with protective framing around the rider, while another adds a roof for even more enclosure.

It’s a fascinating approach because motorcycles have traditionally relied largely on the rider wearing the protection. Helmets, jackets, gloves, boots and sometimes airbag vests form the safety system, while the motorcycle itself generally offers little physical protection during a crash.

The X Cruiser effectively flips part of that equation by building some of the protective structure into the vehicle itself.

There’s an important caveat here, though. Segway specifically notes that its descriptions refer to the vehicle’s current design and equipment and do not mean it has completed automotive-style crash certification. Final equipment and certification will depend on individual markets, so it sounds like the company is holding short of making any major certification claims. Still though, it’s easy to see how having what is effectively a racing seat and roll cage surrounding the rider could seriously contribute to better protection in a crash. Just remember to keep your hands and feet within the vehicle at all times.

And unlike plenty of wild EICMA showpieces, this one isn’t merely destined to live under convention-center spotlights. Segway says the X Cruiser has a confirmed mass-production plan, with launches planned for China and Europe between 2027 and 2028. There’s no US availability announcement yet.

Underneath all that protective hardware is a fairly serious electric touring platform. Segway is using its CTB (cell-to-body) battery integration to help improve structural rigidity and battery packaging, with the company targeting nearly 200 km (124 miles) of range.

European versions are expected to feature 4.5 kW Type 2 AC charging, while the Chinese version will offer optional higher-power DC fast charging. The bike rolls on 15-inch front and 14-inch rear wheels wearing Michelin City Grip tires, and riders get a 10.25-inch TFT display along with an optional 55-liter electrically operated top box.

Interestingly, the X Cruiser also incorporates certain two-wheeler intellectual property and know-how licensed from BMW Group, though Segway stresses that it is responsible for the vehicle’s development, integration, validation, production and certification.

The X Cruiser may be the weirdest – and thus perhaps the most interesting – of Segway’s EICMA debuts, but it was far from alone.

The company also unveiled the Segway Orca Concept, a futuristic high-performance electric maxi-scooter concept built around an 800V electrical architecture and a nearly 20 kWh battery.

Segway is targeting up to 300 km (186 miles) of range, a 0-100 km/h (0-62 mph) time of 4.5 seconds, and the ability to add 200 km (124 miles) of range in 20 minutes. The concept also features front and rear multi-link suspension, electronically controlled multi-mode damping and a battery-integrated CTB chassis. Those figures are engineering targets rather than promised production specifications, and Segway currently describes the Orca strictly as a concept.

Its a BMW C1 reborn as electric! They were a bit of a cult thing, but underpowered for the weight. Never made it to the USA.

The biggest benefit is not really safety, its comfort.

Then there’s Segway’s expanding X Series, which moves the focus away from urban riding and toward dirt. The lineup includes the Xaber X1000 and Xaber 350, along with different Xaber 300 variants for the US and European markets. Segway is also partnering with Michelin for its Dakar Rally Factory Team, using the brutal rally environment as a real-world development and validation platform for electric off-road motorcycles.

Taken together, it’s quite the showing from a company whose name many people still associate primarily with those funny two-wheeled self-balancing machines from the early 2000s.

Segway has already expanded heavily into electric scooters, e-bikes, go-karts and powersports vehicles. Now it seems increasingly serious about becoming an electric motorcycle company as well.

And if motorcycles with roll cages, roofs and seatbelts are part of that future, things could get pretty interesting… pretty quickly!

#4765. The 8 Best Men's Pajamas, Tested by Style Editors

PJ sets by Tommy John and Cozy Earth came out on top in our testing.

AS MUCH AS I love playing dress-up for the office, the second I get home I’m counting down to that moment when I can peel off the suit pants, kick the loafers across the room, and finally feel like a human. Don’t get me wrong, I’m a diehard cozy-hoodie-and-sweats guy (they’re my unofficial uniform for bodega runs and morning coffee walks). But when it’s time to shut my brain off and wind down, pajamas are the endgame. There’s something about slipping into a matching set that taps into that childhood sleepover and Saturday morning cartoons feeling—except I’m an adult who appreciates soft fabrics and a decent bedtime.

Most guys tumble into bed in whatever they happen to be wearing—an old tee, boxers, or absolutely nothing if you're feeling…efficient. But hear me out: investing in the best men’s pajamas is one of those tiny grown-up upgrades that makes a huge difference. They make you look more put-together, keep you warm if you run cold at night, and make bedtime feel less like a crash landing and more like a proper wind-down. Some of our editors even pack PJs for vacations because slipping into a proper set in a hotel bed feels downright luxurious.

If you're tired of tossing and turning in your worn-out sweatpants or boxers, we’ve got you covered. Our Men’s Health fashion team and I have tested more than 30 pairs since 2020 and curated the best of the bunch. From classic button-down sets in breathable cotton to slim jogger-style pajama bottoms with stretch at the waistband, side seams, and knees—it’s all here. Whether you're reserving the weekend to lie around like a couch potato or catching up on some serious Z's, these pajamas are your ticket to bedtime bliss.

This list of eight men’s pajamas checks every box—perfect for yourself or as a thoughtful, stylish gift.

Over the past six years, Men’s Health editors have tested every pajama set worth sleeping in, but very few deliver dreamy comfort and high quality like Tommy John. That’s because the brand’s Second Skin Set, a pocket tee and pant combo, earns its name with a silky modal-spandex blend that feels buttery smooth, stretches just right, and breathes all night.

I’ve worn this all year and it's still my go-to for bedtime. The fabric drapes cleanly off the body with a relaxed fit that flatters without clinging. I found it less warm than flannel pajamas, and it never itches or pills, even after dozens of washes. Plus, the stretch makes it convenient for spreading out across the couch, reaching for the remote, or heading downstairs for coffee. What also sold me on this pair was the waistband on the pants. It’s built with a nonrestrictive band that stays put without digging into my waist or folding over.

I usually air dry mine so it lasts longer, but even on a low tumble, it’s resistant to fading and shrinking. The set runs a bit warm for guys who sleep hot in peak summer. It’s not heavy, but it’s not as light as a linen or jersey knit. But for that second-skin softness, Tommy John’s set makes every other pair feel like a backup.

If you sleep hot, our editors recommend Cozy Earth’s set because it will keep you cool from the very first night. The T-shirt and shorts combo uses silky viscose from bamboo that’s soft and regulates your temperature. Our Grooming Editor, Sean Zucker said their bedroom “feels like a sauna most nights,” yet it kept him dry and comfortable until morning. It feels just as cozy as cotton, breathes well, and doesn’t trap heat like flannel.

The relaxed fit is another win. The tee hangs loosely through the chest and shoulders, while the shorts drape neatly and never ride up when you shift in bed. When Zucker bent down to grab slippers or kicked the covers off, the fabric didn’t tug or twist. After more than eight washes, the fabric still looks fresh from the day he opened the pack.

We tested it across every season and found it stays cool in the summer, cozy in spring and fall. While this T-shirt and shorts set looks more like cozy underwear than traditional PJs, we happily take that trade for how ridiculously soft and cool it feels.

This Hanes PJ set punches above its price point, delivering comfort you’d expect from options twice the cost. The fabric feels light, but neither flimsy nor scratchy. Similar to the brand’s special X-temp underwear, it’s produced with a breathable cotton that feels soft against the skin. After six washes, we noticed no shrinking or pilling. While it’s available in solid colored styles, our favorite is the grey textured pattern with contrast piping, which lends a festive holiday vibe without feeling like a costume.

Fit-wise, it runs roomier than J.Crew’s version, but doesn’t leave you swimming in fabric. I lounged on the couch, took a post-dinner nap, and curled up with a book, and the set stayed comfortable throughout it all. The fabric isn’t thick enough to keep you toasty if the AC is blasting, but it won’t make you sweat either.

I love this pajama pant because it has flexibility that lets me move freely. Since the cotton-rayon fabric is blended with elastane, I’ve been able to meditate, stretch in the morning, and even fold laundry, without it losing shape. Even though the pant has some give, it still has structure. The material has a buttery Skims feel, with a flowy drape and just enough weight so it hangs neatly without clinging.

While it almost resembles your favorite sweatpant, it’s not bulky or heavy. I wouldn't necessarily run errands around town in it, though; I would throw it on with a hoodie to grab my matcha latte at a nearby coffee shop.

I love a henley because its flattering neckline lets you control your airflow, and Eberjey makes the best one for sleeping. It’s made of a velvety soft modal fabric, which is lightweight and breathable. My apartment runs hot at night, but the set kept me from waking up in sweat puddles. Although the material clings to my chest, the neckline allows for extra breathability.

Despite the leg fit being slightly tapered, this option still feels great even on beefy thighs. The top is more relaxed, so it’s forgiving in the stomach if you’ve had a late-night burger. Thanks to the spandex blend, I found the material to be stretchier than Brooks Brothers’ cotton fabric, so I could lean back in the recliner chair and not feel restricted. Also: the pockets are pretty deep, so you can carry around your phone, if you need to make a run to the kitchen for a late-night snack.

I wore these cotton pajamas during a friend’s birthday weekend getaway, and they were comfortable enough to lounge around and sleep in. The white-and-black color combination is a classic, but the subtle piping gives the two-piece set a little more personality than your standard white pajamas. Just be sure to wash them with like colors to keep that crisp white looking fresh. The lightweight, breathable cotton feels soft against my skin, almost like how my bedsheets feel after they’ve just come out of the dryer. The fit is relaxed through the body and thighs but still neat enough that I wouldn’t think twice about stepping outside to chat with a neighbor or walk the dog.

The Airbnb we stayed in ran a little warm at night, but I never felt like I was overheating in this set. The fabric isn’t as flexible as Eberjey’s, but it still gives me enough room to bend down to pick something up, reach for something, or grab the newspaper without feeling restricted.

J.Crew makes a pajama set with a timeless style that always looks sharp. Its OG-looking button closure, rounded collars, and white piping give Home Alone vibes for grownups. I tested it and can confirm: it’s perfect for colder days when all you want to do is snuggle up and stay warm. The fabric blend of organic cotton, modal, and elastane feels way softer and stretchier than standard cotton. It has a smooth, broken-in texture that moves with you instead of bunching or clinging.

The top has just enough structure to look neat without feeling stiff, and—huge plus—you can lift your arms without the hem creeping up. I’m 5'8" and the pants have a streamlined fit with an ideal length and never catch under my feet. After a few washes, I noticed slight shrinkage, but the overall shape and softness remained strong. This set looks polished enough that you won’t hesitate to step outside to take out the trash or go grab the newspaper.

If you want pajamas that feel like getting a hug from a teddy bear, consider this plaid flannel design from L.L.Bean. They’re made from long-staple cotton and the flannel is brushed eight times on each side for an ultra-soft feel that makes slipping into bed on a cold night that much better. Think fireplace going, slippers on, and absolutely nowhere else to be. The classic plaid pattern also reminds me of that nostalgic, holiday-season vibe, making it a great pick for matching Christmas pajamas with the family.

Beyond the cozy factor, the set has a relaxed fit through the chest, sleeves, and waist, so you have plenty of room to move around without feeling bundled up in excess fabric. The pants sit at your natural waist with a drawstring to tighten and fall into a breathable straight leg. The top also has a chest pocket where you can rest your phone or remote control. Plus, the set comes in regular, short, and tall sizes, so you can find a fit that works for your frame.

If you’re a hot sleeper, look for cotton, bamboo, or modal. If you tend to get cold at night, opt for fleece or flannel. Below, we've broken down what to expect from each type of material.

A classic choice, cotton is lightweight, breathable, and super soft. It’s perfect for year-round wear, traditional button-down sets, and those who love the feel of natural fibers.

It’s silky, lightweight, and feels like second skin. It’s also stretchy, but that depends on the knit and fabric blend. Pajamas with a bit of spandex or elastane provide stretch so you can move easily while sleeping.

Nobody wants PJs that feel restrictive, but you also don’t want to look like you’re swimming in fabric. Aim for a fit that’s relaxed but still polished. Whether you’re into classic button-down sets or modern loungewear vibes, pick a style that makes you feel good lounging around the house.

When it comes to the perfect pair of pajamas, some special features can make a huge impact. For one, pockets are essential for your phone, remote, tissues, or late-night snack (but please, never in bed). An elastic waistband with a drawstring cord lets you adjust the fit to your exact liking. This way, they will stay in place and not dig into your skin, no matter how much you toss and turn at night.

When it came to hunting down the ultimate pajamas, we didn’t mess around. Led by Style and Reviews Director Christian Gollayan, our fashion team curated a wide range of men’s pajama sets from various brands and put each one to the test. We focused on everything that matters—fabric feel, fit, style, durability, year-round wearability, and those little extras that take PJs from comfortable to next-level cozy.

Then we got hands-on. Each set went through real-life scenarios: lounging on the couch after a long day, whipping up breakfast, stretching, bending, and all the everyday around-the-house moves you actually do. We paid close attention to breathability, softness, and how well the pants and tops moved with you.

#4764. This Is How Fast You Should Walk to Help Lower Your Risk of Death

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

New research shows that how fast you walk, whether measured in a clinical test or through daily activity, can help predict your risk of dying from any cause.

The study compared two ways of measuring walking: a short walking speed test conducted in a clinic and the step rate people take in their everyday lives, measured with a wrist-worn device.

Both measures were linked to mortality risk and showed similar ability to predict it.

The findings, published on October 23 in JAMA Network Open, could help doctors and researchers choose the best method for assessing health risks in different settings.

The study was part of the Whitehall II accelerometer substudy in the United Kingdom.

It included 4,067 participants, mostly males, with an average age of about 69 years. About one-third of the subjects were female.

The researchers collected data from January 2012 to December 2013 and followed up through August 2024.

To measure clinical walking speed, participants completed a standard walking test. They walked a marked 2.44-meter course at their usual pace. The test was repeated three times, and the average speed in meters per second was used for analysis. Participants who normally used a cane were allowed to use it during the test.

For free-living walking measurements, participants wore a wrist-worn GENEActiv accelerometer for 9 consecutive days. This device recorded movement at a high frequency and used special software to detect walking episodes and count steps.

From this data, two key measures of walking cadence were calculated: the median walking cadence (the middle value of steps per minute during walking periods) and the 95th-percentile walking cadence (a higher step rate indicating brisk walking). The study also calculated the average number of daily steps.

The researchers additionally gathered information on factors known to affect mortality, such as:

National death records were used to identify deaths during the follow-up period.

Statistical methods were then used to estimate the risk of death associated with walking speed and cadence while accounting for other risk factors.

The models were adjusted step-by-step: starting with no adjustments, then adding sociodemographic factors, behavioral factors, and finally health-related factors.

The ability of walking measures to predict mortality was assessed using a statistical measure.

The study also examined differences between males and females.

The researchers additionally conducted analyses to test how well the results held up when they excluded early deaths, looked at subgroups by age and health status, and used different definitions of walking cadence.

During a median follow-up of nearly 12 years, 739 participants died.

The average clinical walking speed of participants was 1.2 meters per second. The median walking cadence during daily life was about 75 steps per minute, and the 95th percentile walking cadence was about 112 steps per minute.

The study found only a weak correlation between clinical walking speed and free-living walking cadence, meaning the two measures do not strongly reflect the same walking behavior. However, both measures were independently associated with a lower risk of death.

After adjusting for age, sex, lifestyle, and health factors, for every standard increase in clinical walking speed, the risk of death was 23% lower.

Similarly, higher median and 95th-percentile walking cadences were associated with 17% and 18% lower risks of death, respectively.

When examining how well these walking measures predicted mortality, each on its own showed modest predictive ability.

Adding clinical walking speed to a model with other known risk factors slightly improved mortality prediction, while adding free-living walking cadence also improved prediction, albeit to a similar degree to that of clinical walking speed.

Combining clinical walking speed with free-living walking parameters provided a small boost in predictive ability, but the effect was not significant after accounting for detailed health factors.

The study also found that walking speed and cadence had similar predictive power for both men and women, although the overall prediction models performed slightly better for women.

Several sensitivity analyses supported the main findings. Results were consistent when excluding early deaths, focusing on healthier or older participants, and using different ways to define walking cadence.

Overall, this study suggests that clinical walking speed tests and free-living walking cadence measurements from wrist-worn devices are both useful in predicting all-cause mortality risk. They provide similar information but reflect different aspects of walking behavior.

The choice between methods may depend on the purpose of the assessment, available resources, and the context in which the measurement is taken.

Neha Sabharwal, PT, DPT, a physical therapist and director of rehabilitation specializing in geriatric mobility and functional decline at Vintage Faire Nursing and Rehabilitation Center in Modesto, CA, said that walking speed helps predict longevity because it’s an indicator of someone’s overall health.

“Walking is something most of us do without thinking about it, but it requires several body systems to work together,” she told Healthline. “Your heart and lungs have to keep up, your muscles need to produce enough force, and your brain has to coordinate each step while keeping you balanced.”

Sabharwal, who wasn’t involved in the study, said that in her work, she pays attention to when someone starts walking more slowly than before.

“It is easy to dismiss that change as part of getting older, but there may be something else going on,” she said. This could include muscle weakness, pain, reduced endurance, balance problems, or underlying medical conditions.

According to Sabharwal, the current study is valuable because it suggests that useful information about people’s movement can be obtained outside a clinical setting.

However, she cautioned against misinterpreting the findings to mean that simply walking faster will make you live longer.

“People who naturally walk faster may already have better underlying health,” said Sabharwal.

“I would be less concerned about whether someone walks faster than their neighbor and more interested in whether they are walking slower than they did six months ago,” she said.

Theodore Strange, MD, chairman of medicine at Northwell Staten Island University Hospital and senior vice president of the Metro Market Region at Northwell Health, shared some insights for those who may notice their walking speed has declined. Strange wasn’t involved in the study.

“I mean, if it’s slowing down because a week or two ago, you were walking up a flight of steps with no problem, and now, you’re having some shortness of breath, I think it should be evaluated,” he told Healthline.

Strange added that if you’re experiencing aches or pains that weren’t there before, you should consult a healthcare professional, as they can make exercise more difficult.

It’s also essential to manage any chronic diseases that you have so that you can exercise as well as possible within the constraints of your condition, he said.

“And I think slow and steady wins the race here,” said Strange. He suggests monitoring your walking with a device like a pedometer and progressively increasing your steps.

“Everybody talks about 10,000 steps a day. I think the most recent studies show probably 7,000 to 8,000 is adequate,” he said. You can start where you are and work your way up gradually.

Strange further noted that physical therapy can sometimes be helpful if you have issues with gait mechanics, balance, or strength. Additionally, you might benefit from exercise that is tailored to your condition, for example, if you’ve had a stroke.

Finally, Strange advised stretching before and after exercise to keep your muscles moving.

“I go back to adequate nutrition and hydration being important,” he said. You want to make sure you are adequately supporting your body’s ability to exercise, said Strange.
